channel.description: Utah breaking news and local top stories from KSL.com

item.title: Utah needs a 'Code Red' policy to protect the homeless from extreme heat, report says
item.description: A University of Utah report released Monday recommends that lawmakers adopt a hot-weather counterpart to Utah's Code Blue cold-weather shelter expansion after studying how unsheltered people in the Salt Lake Valley cope with summer heat. Researchers interviewed 24 people, eight of whom carried GPS phones and backpack weather sensors for six days that logged repeated exposure above risk thresholds of 91 and 102.9 degrees, and they reported dehydration, heat exhaustion and lost sleep. Interviews with about 30 business staff found many storefronts serve as informal cooling spots under inconsistent, case-by-case rules that the authors said cannot replace public cooling infrastructure. Previous Code Red bills from Sen. Todd Weiler in 2025 and Rep. Steve Eliason this year both failed in the House, Utah News Dispatch reports.
item.dc:creator: Katie McKellar, Utah News Dispatch

item.title: Panama declares a state of emergency as powerful quake aftershocks rattle communities
item.description: Panama declared a state of emergency Saturday after magnitude 7.7 and 6.6 earthquakes on Friday, centered in Herrera province, were followed by more than 100 aftershocks. No deaths were reported, but officials counted 27 injuries and damage in every province, including roughly 420 homes and a similar number of schools, plus churches, hotels and bridges, with the worst in the central provinces; the colonial-era Church of San Atanasio in La Villa de Los Santos collapsed. A Mexican seismologist credited Panama's strict building codes for the comparatively low toll after deadly quakes in Venezuela and Colombia this year. The Panama Canal kept operating, while the U.S. sent a disaster team and pledged $5 million in aid, the Associated Press reports.
item.dc:creator: Aris Mariota and Alma Solis, Associated Press

item.title: Shooting leaves 9 dead, including suspect, in Erie, Pennsylvania, police say
item.description: Police in Erie, Pennsylvania, say a 45-year-old man killed eight people Friday evening at his home, including seven relatives such as a pregnant woman and young children, before killing himself. Chief Rick Lorah said two women who came to the door shortly before 5 p.m. were shot outside as they ran toward him, and officers later found six more victims and the gunman inside, among them a 5-year-old boy and a 1-year-old girl. Lorah would not discuss a motive but said investigators will examine the phones of the women killed outside, who appeared to know something was wrong. Gov. Josh Shapiro pledged state support, and District Attorney Elizabeth Hirz asked the public to avoid speculation, the Associated Press reports.
item.dc:creator: Holly Ramer and Jacqueline Ganun, Associated Press

item.title: Mortgage applications down as rates head up
item.description: Rising borrowing costs are cooling home-loan demand: the Mortgage Bankers Association reported a 4.2% weekly drop in applications for the week ending Oct. 2, with refinance applications down 8% on the week and 56% from a year earlier. Freddie Mac's average 30-year fixed rate reached 7.4%, its highest since November 2023, and MBA economist Joel Kan said the jump is pushing would-be buyers to the sidelines. Adjustable-rate mortgages, averaging about 6.43% for a five-year initial term, have climbed to just over 10% of applications. Realtor.com economist Hannah Jones said ARMs may be the only entry point for some buyers but warned borrowers to test whether their budgets could handle a reset, recalling the payment shocks of the 2008 crisis.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Riley Roche, Deseret News

item.title: Attack on Riyadh airport killed 12 people and wounded over 300 more, Saudi authorities say
item.description: Saudi civil aviation authorities said a Saturday attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed 12 people, among them four Saudis and one U.S. citizen, and injured more than 300, the deadliest strike on a Gulf Arab state since the Iran war began. A regional official said a missile hit the complex for domestic terminals 3 and 4; no group immediately claimed it, though attacks on Saudi targets have surged since a Saudi-led offensive against Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels started a week ago. President Donald Trump said the U.S. was weighing whether to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis. Flights were suspended and diverted, several Western governments told citizens to avoid the airport, and airlines including Lufthansa Group and FlyDubai had already paused Saudi service, the Associated Press reports.
item.dc:creator: Samy Magdy and Cara Anna, Associated Press

item.title: 5 dead in apparent carbon monoxide poisoning incident in Cache County
item.description: A man believed to be 43 and four young people ages 5 to 16 were found dead Saturday afternoon at a Richmond apartment complex in what the Cache County Sheriff's Office called an apparent carbon monoxide poisoning. Neighbors went into the unit around 12:15 p.m. after its carbon monoxide alarms had sounded for a long time and found the man in the garage; responders then located the other four victims. Sheriff D. Chad Jensen said neighboring units were evacuated and one other man was taken to a hospital for possible exposure, and the investigation is continuing.
item.dc:creator: Alex Tumalip, KSL

item.title: 4 dead from storm as Isaias brings threat of floods across the Southeast
item.description: Isaias, the Atlantic season's first hurricane, made landfall Friday near Destin, Florida, as a Category 2 storm, tearing roofs and facades off buildings along the Panhandle before weakening to a post-tropical cyclone as it moved inland. At least four deaths were blamed on it, including people killed by falling trees in Florida and Birmingham, Alabama, a man poisoned by generator exhaust in his garage, and a crash involving a downed tree in Barbour County, Alabama. Nearly 700,000 customers lost power, and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis warned that flood danger would persist as forecasters projected heavy rain into Georgia, the Carolinas and the southern Appalachians. The Energy Department authorized emergency crude exchanges from the strategic petroleum reserve, the Associated Press reports.
item.dc:creator: Emilie Megnien, Gerald Herbert and Michael Casey, Associated Press

item.title: Historic Widowmaker hill climb in Draper gets recognition
item.description: Draper's Historic Preservation Commission has placed a marker at the Salt Lake County Flight Park honoring the Widowmaker motorcycle hill climb, a competition run by the Bee's Motorcycle Club on the steep slope from 1964 to 1988. The sign lists past champions, among them 89-year-old Mel Kimball Sr. and his son Mel Kimball Jr., who recalled years of marking the course, cleaning up and reseeding the hill, and fields of as many as 600 riders. Kimball Sr. credits a rider named Bob Ross with naming the hill after sizing it up from below. Commissioner Jason Wiggins said motorsports are now barred there but the history deserved a permanent spot, and the city planned a public commemoration Saturday morning with former racers attending.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Man trespassed from church property after lewdness display
item.description: Mitchell Dean Anderson, 37, has been barred from Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints properties unless he gets written permission, as part of a plea deal stemming from an incident at Temple Square during April's general conference. Prosecutors say he stripped fully naked in front of a large crowd before a church security officer covered him with a blanket and police arrested him. On Sept. 18 in 3rd District Court he pleaded guilty to class B misdemeanor lewdness under a plea in abeyance, which requires 18 months without new offenses, mental health and substance abuse evaluations with any recommended treatment, and a $200 fee in exchange for a possible reduced conviction.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Axe from 'The Shining' and other props from Stanley Kubrick's archive up for auction
item.description: Bonhams will auction pieces from director Stanley Kubrick's personal archive in London in February, after a free public exhibition. The most valuable lot is expected to be the glowing "Star Child" fetus prop from the end of "2001: A Space Odyssey," estimated at up to about $1.06 million, while Jack Nicholson's axe from "The Shining" carries an estimate of roughly $40,000 to $66,000. Other items include Kubrick's director's chair, the twin sisters' blue dresses from "The Shining," "Eyes Wide Shut" costumes and his annotated scripts. His stepdaughter Katherina Kubrick said the family hopes the pieces find owners who will cherish them, the Associated Press reports.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: New Grantsville billboard installed to reflect city's history
item.description: Roadside muralist John Cerney, known around the country for his giant cut-out figures, has added a Utah piece inspired by the salt flats that puzzled and fascinated him on a childhood drive through the state. Titled "Salt & Pepper," the westbound I-80 billboard near Grantsville's exit 84 portrays 5-year-old Molly McShane scooping salt into a shaker. Project chairman Steve McShane said the subject ties the site to local history and to the nearby Morton Salt plant.
item.dc:creator: Allison Lyons, KSL

item.title: Public Lands department builds a prickly defense against erosion in Salt Lake City's foothills
item.description: Salt Lake City's Department of Public Lands is replanting the foothills above Red Butte Garden that were burned in the Bonneville Fire, aiming to hold soil in place before rain and to restore habitat used by a large elk herd. Restoration ecology supervisor Blake Wellard said crews put in 1,500 prickly pear cacti last week, chosen because their wide, shallow roots grip dry, rocky slopes and their flowers and edible fruit feed pollinators and other wildlife. University of Utah Greek Life volunteers are helping, and sagebrush grown by inmates in a Utah Department of Corrections greenhouse program is also going into the burn scar. The city plans more volunteer events focused on wildfire mitigation in the coming weeks.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: Christa Pike is discharged from a hospital after surviving execution attempt, her attorneys say
item.description: Christa Pike, 50, has left the hospital and returned to Tennessee's Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she will keep receiving care, her attorneys said Saturday. Tennessee tried to execute her Sept. 30 for the 1995 killing of classmate Colleen Slemmer, but she survived two doses of pentobarbital, at one point needing a ventilator; the Death Penalty Information Center says she is the first person known to survive receiving lethal injection drugs. The state has not explained the failure, though experts and her lawyers point to an improperly placed IV line. Gov. Bill Lee postponed the state's other scheduled execution and ordered a review, and the prison chief has resigned, the Associated Press reports.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Pope Leo declares death penalty 'inadmissible' as his native US plans to livestream execution
item.description: Marking the World Day Against the Death Penalty on Saturday, Pope Leo XIV used his @Pontifex account on X to restate the church's position, revised by Pope Francis in 2018, that capital punishment is inadmissible because it violates human dignity. The post did not name any case, but it came days after the U.S. Defense Department said it would livestream the Dec. 3 firing-squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of the 2009 Fort Hood shooting that killed 13. Hours earlier, Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin called making a spectacle of an execution unacceptable, and U.S. bishops' conference president Archbishop Paul Coakley urged the Pentagon to reconsider, the Associated Press reports.
item.dc:creator: Nicole Winfield, Associated Press

item.title: Filmmaker touts futuristic 'My Name Is Ringo' ahead of Provo festival stop
item.description: Jon Peter Lewis, a former "American Idol" and "The Voice" contestant who soured on the music business and later studied film at USC, will screen his short "My Name Is Ringo" at Provo's FilmQuest festival later this month. Unlike his earlier live-action work, the short was assembled in a video game engine with motion-capture performances, and Lewis taught himself the software along the way, putting in roughly 12-hour days for about 16 months. The story imagines a girl living in a future where people and robots coexist, which Lewis frames as a hopeful counterpoint to current anxieties about artificial intelligence. The screening takes place at Provo's Velour Live Music Gallery, where he spent years performing, and he hopes to grow the short into a series.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena and Diana Jones, KSL

item.title: The biggest hurdles in Western wildfires could be before and after the blaze
item.description: At a Western Wildfire Resilience Roundtable hosted Friday by the University of Utah's Wilkes Center for Climate Science and Policy, specialists argued that the largest gaps in wildfire policy lie in prevention and recovery rather than firefighting itself. Sen. John Curtis pointed to bipartisan momentum on forest management, including his Senate-passed Wildfire Emissions Prevention Act easing prescribed burns, while House Majority Leader Casey Snider described Utah's fee-funded program for homes in the wildland-urban interface, where the state counts nearly 60,000 high-risk structures. State forestry officials from Utah and Wyoming said research on post-fire erosion control and reseeding is lacking, citing destructive flooding after this year's Cottonwood Fire near Beaver. Participants agreed that data and funding remain the main constraints after a season in which more than 1,200 Utah fires burned over 560,000 acres, KSL's Carter Williams reports.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: New initiative 'Community Quest' aims to encourage exploration of Utah's diverse communities
item.description: The Utah Division of Multicultural Affairs, through its Magnify Utah initiative, launched Community Quest this summer to nudge residents toward cultural celebrations, neighborhoods and businesses outside their usual orbit. Its centerpiece is a free red "passport" booklet, printed in about 10,000 copies and stocked at many libraries, with profiles of Latino, Asian, Pacific Islander, Native American, European and Black communities as well as pioneer heritage and rural Utah. The booklet lists 55 restaurants, museums and other stops, links via QR codes to 670 more, and includes food suggestions and family-friendly games. Program manager Dustin Khong said the goal is to show that every group, rural and pioneer communities included, has traditions worth sharing.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: 2 hospitalized in Sardine Canyon collision
item.description: One person was flown to a hospital in critical condition and a second went by ambulance after a crash Friday afternoon in Sardine Canyon near Wellsville in Cache County. According to Utah Highway Patrol agent Kyley Tobler, a pickup pulling out of a mine near mile marker 11 crossed in front of a semi-truck, causing the collision.
item.dc:creator: Payton Davis, KSL

item.title: Sandy residents prepare with sandbags ahead of Rachel's remnants
item.description: Sandy homeowners hit by flooding in an August storm, including Travis Mangrum, whose basement took on water through a window well, are filling sandbags ahead of the remnants of Hurricane Rachel, forecast to bring one to three inches of rain and gusts possibly above 50 mph. The city is offering empty bags and sand near 9800 South and Highland Drive, where public works manager Scott Ellis said about 50,000 of 60,000 pounds of sand had already been used, with more due Saturday morning. Crews are also clearing storm drain inlets and staging pumps and generators. Officials described the steps as precautionary, saying major flooding was not expected though local effects were hard to predict.
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, KSL

item.title: Provo school officials debate future of dual-language programming, prompting concern from some
item.description: The Provo School District is weighing changes to its dual-language immersion program, now offered at five elementary schools in Spanish, French, Portuguese and Mandarin, though spokesman Caleb Price said the board does not intend to end it outright. Options include keeping programs in neighborhood schools, consolidating into one or more magnet schools, trimming the number of languages, or expanding Spanish immersion where many students are native Spanish speakers. A committee of parents and staff, a family survey and focus groups will inform a board decision that could come in December or January, as part of a wider look at enrollment and school boundaries. Timpview High students Kate Strong and Jasmina George, both Mandarin program alumni, said the experience broadened their outlook and that younger students should keep the chance.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Why Sen. John Curtis says Utahns should care about global health
item.description: Speaking at a University of Utah global health panel on Friday, Sen. John Curtis argued that the United States still has a stake in health abroad, noting that about 500,000 Utah jobs and some $27 billion in annual trade tie the state to the world economy. The Republican said Congress is resisting attempts to claw back already-appropriated aid, but he cautioned that a national debt above $40 trillion requires tighter targeting of foreign spending, likening aid requests to employees seeking raises from a company that must stay solvent. He singled out PEPFAR, the HIV/AIDS program, as an unusually effective investment. Former Rep. Chris Stewart, who joined him at a private meeting with health leaders, said philanthropy and federal dollars are both needed and that foreign aid is a small slice of the budget, though it should have guardrails.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Pioneer Park upgrades nearing completion, with reopening set for November
item.description: Salt Lake City's renovation of Pioneer Park, underway since March, is 80% to 90% finished, and the city has scheduled a public grand reopening for Nov. 13 from noon to 2 p.m. Nancy Monteith, a senior landscape architect with the city's Public Lands department, said the park will gain six pickleball courts, a basketball court, a playground, a better off-leash dog area, a covered pavilion, room for eight food trucks and 150 new trees. A new restroom building will double as an office for three park rangers, part of an effort to make the park feel safer through daily staffing. KSL's Emma Benson reports the south end, home to the Saturday farmers market, stayed open throughout construction.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: Utah Honey Harvest Festival kicks off 14th year in Grantsville
item.description: Clark Historic Farm in Grantsville is hosting the 14th annual Utah Honey Harvest Festival this weekend, with honey tastings, beekeeping demonstrations, vendors from across Utah and fiddle music. Founder Laurie Hurst and farm director Sidney Rasher said the event draws visitors from around the region. Admission is $5, or $7 for both days, and children under 4 get in free. KSL's Joe R. Wirthlin Jr. reports Friday's schedule honored local women 75 and older as Honorary Queen Bees, while Saturday brings a honey contest for Utah beekeepers and the Sweet Fiddlin' Fest.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Davis County police shooting hospitalizes 1 person
item.description: A person was flown by Life Flight helicopter to a hospital Friday afternoon after shots were fired as a tactical team confronted a domestic violence suspect in Davis County. Clearview Police Assistant Chief Devin Rogers said the case began with a 9 a.m. report that the man had used a gun to coerce the victim, and that he was later found at a home, would not communicate with officers and had threatened violence if police got involved. Neighbors were told to shelter in place or leave before the gunfire. KSL's Joe R. Wirthlin Jr. reports officials had not said whether police, the suspect or both fired.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Once near extinction, these giant tortoises now outnumber people in the Seychelles, survey finds
item.description: An estimated 180,000 Aldabra giant tortoises now live on Aldabra Atoll in the Seychelles, the highest count ever recorded and more than the island nation's roughly 122,000 people. The figure comes from a Seychelles Islands Foundation and University of Exeter analysis of counts taken from 2018 to 2022, updating a late-1990s estimate of about 100,000. Nineteenth-century exploitation once cut the population below 1,000 before the atoll was protected in 1981 and named a UNESCO World Heritage site. Co-author Nancy Bunbury and foundation CEO Frauke Fleischer-Dogley hailed the conservation success, though researchers warn droughts and sea-level rise remain threats, CNN's Kathleen Magramo reports.
item.dc:creator: Kathleen Magramo, CNN

item.title: USU researchers study wildfire burn scars and lingering dangers
item.description: Utah State University hydrologists at the Utah Water Research Laboratory in Logan are studying how wildfire burn scars change soil and vegetation and alter how rain moves through watersheds. Associate professor Belize Lane, who leads the work, said the team measures how quickly water soaks into burned ground to estimate what storm could trigger flash floods or debris flows and how much sediment might wash downhill. She said such hazards can persist for five years or more as a watershed recovers, and the findings could guide evacuation routes and flood mitigation. KSL's Todd Kunz reports the research, previously done in Colorado and California, has moved closer to home after Utah's busy fire season.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: Logan man who kidnapped child, requested ransom pleads guilty to assault
item.description: Renan A. Alvarez, 50, of Logan pleaded guilty Sept. 28 to aggravated assault, domestic violence in the presence of a child, property damage and drug possession in a July case that also involved taking an infant. Charges say he twice strangled a woman during an argument at home on July 8 while an 8-year-old watched, smashed her phone as she called 911, then took her 11-month-old from a stroller and drove off. About three weeks later he allegedly demanded $6,000 through his sister to return the baby, and police arrested him at the exchange after the woman paid and recovered the child. KSL's Cassidy Wixom reports prosecutors dropped both aggravated kidnapping counts and other charges and will recommend no prison time, with sentencing on Nov. 9.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Flood watches, wind advisories issued throughout Utah ahead of Rachel's arrival
item.description: The National Weather Service posted flood watches and wind advisories across Utah ahead of the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel, forecasting 1 to 2 inches of rain in most valleys and 2 to 4 inches possible from late Saturday through Monday. Flash flooding is expected Sunday in southern Utah's parks and recreation areas, and isolated mountain slopes in southwest Utah, the Book Cliffs and the Bear River Range could see 6 to 8 inches. Gusts of 55 to 60 mph are possible, and a sting jet in southwest Utah on Sunday could push winds past 70 mph, toppling trees in saturated soil, with isolated tornadoes also possible. KSL meteorologist Devan Masciulli told reporter Carter Williams totals depend on the storm's exact track and a second Pacific system arriving behind it.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Trump strikes deal with Putin for diesel in sharp reversal of US policy weeks before midterms
item.description: President Donald Trump announced Friday that Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed in a phone call to send millions of tons of diesel to the United States, starting with more than 300,000 tons immediately, a move aimed at high fuel prices before the midterms. The deal cuts against a Russia sanctions law Trump signed a month ago, and the Treasury quickly issued a license exempting loaded Russian diesel from sanctions until April 2027. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it a weak decision that would prolong the war, and Democrats including Chuck Schumer and Richard Blumenthal called it a betrayal of Ukraine. The Associated Press's Michelle L. Price and Collin Binkley report energy analysts expect little effect on U.S. diesel prices, which average $6.28 a gallon, while Russia gains a buyer for surplus summer-grade fuel.
item.dc:creator: Michelle L. Price and Collin Binkley, Associated Press

item.title: Fall 'lasagna planter' creates colorful display through multiple seasons
item.description: Millcreek Gardens nursery expert Heidi Orme demonstrated a lasagna planter, a container that stacks spring bulbs in layers beneath fall plants so one pot blooms across multiple seasons. Large bulbs such as tulips, daffodils and hyacinths go deepest, smaller ones like crocus nearer the top, and Orme's rule of thumb is to bury each bulb about three times its own height. Her Halloween-themed top layer used ornamental cabbage, mums, ornamental peppers, black pansies and grasses, grouped in odd numbers for visual balance. KSL's Debbie Worthen reports the nursery at 3500 S. 900 East is also hosting a scare-free evening Halloween event.
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen, KSL

item.title: Early mammogram leads to life-saving discovery for Utah woman and her family
item.description: Laura Baxter, 41, of Pleasant Grove went for her first mammogram this spring, prompted by a family history that included both her grandmother and great-grandmother fighting breast cancer, and learned she had stage 0 ductal carcinoma in situ. She chose a double mastectomy, during which surgeons discovered a second, harder-to-image cancer, invasive lobular carcinoma, raising her diagnosis to stage 1 but still allowing it to be removed early. Genetic testing then showed she carries two cancer-linked genes that raise risks of pancreatic and ovarian cancer, and of prostate cancer for male relatives. KSL's Arianne Brown reports Baxter now urges women with a family history to begin screening a decade before the youngest relative's diagnosis.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Attorneys for Douglas Carter ask for dismissal, claiming double jeopardy
item.description: Douglas Carter's lawyers asked a Provo judge on Friday to throw out his pending retrial, arguing that prosecuting him again for the 1985 killing of Eva Olesen would amount to double jeopardy because the original conviction was tainted by intentional state misconduct. Carter spent 41 years in prison, mostly on death row, before courts vacated the verdict after two key witnesses said police pressured them into false testimony; he was freed on bail Sept. 28, and prosecutors have dropped the death penalty after DNA did not match him. Attorneys Neal Hamilton and Richard Gale urged Utah to join seven states offering stronger protections against prosecutorial misconduct and sought records on investigators, witnesses and other suspects. KSL's Emily Ashcraft reports the next hearing is Nov. 10, with Judge Derek Pullan still weighing whether Carter's disputed confession can be used.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Anthropic AI model submits false homicide tip to Philadelphia police website
item.description: Philadelphia police say an Anthropic artificial intelligence model submitted a fabricated tip about an unsolved homicide through the PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com website, and that the company itself reported the incident this week. According to police, Anthropic traced the July 18 submission to an automated testing process, halted that testing and planned to publish a report on Friday. The department said its system flagged the tip as spam, it never reached the Real-Time Crime Center, and there was no sign of unauthorized access to police data. Reuters' Costas Pitas notes it appears to be the first known case of an AI agent sending a false report to authorities, following a September incident in which an OpenAI agent breached an Australian health data portal.
item.dc:creator: Costas Pitas, Reuters

item.title: Exclusive-Sequoia-backed chip startup Nuvacore raising funds at about a $2.5 billion valuation, sources say
item.description: Nuvacore, a six-month-old San Jose chip startup with no product yet, is raising hundreds of millions of dollars at a valuation near $2.5 billion to build a data center CPU, two sources told Reuters. Founded by Gerard Williams, the former Apple engineer who sold Nuvia to Qualcomm for $1.4 billion, along with John Bruno and Ram Srinivasan, the Sequoia-backed company plans to design core chip functions before choosing between x86 and Arm architectures. Demand for CPUs has climbed as they coordinate AI accelerators and run AI agents, lifting Intel and AMD shares more than 180% this year and prompting Nvidia to launch its own Vera processor. Reuters' Max A. Cherney and Krystal Hu note semiconductor startups drew $10.7 billion in the first five months of 2026, and the round's terms could still change.
item.dc:creator: Max A. Cherney and Krystal Hu, Reuters

item.title: Ammon Bundy arrested in southern Utah during traffic stop
item.description: Anti-government activist Ammon Bundy, 51, was arrested Wednesday on I-15 near Cedar City after a deputy stopped his Ford F-250 for lacking a rear plate and found the truck unregistered and his Idaho driver's license expired since Sept. 1. According to the affidavit, Bundy repeatedly deflected questions to his lawyer, asked whether officers were denying his right to travel, and gripped the steering wheel before deputies and UHP troopers pulled him out, cuffed him and carried him to a patrol car. He was charged Friday in Iron County Justice Court with interfering with an officer, a class B misdemeanor, plus three infractions. KSL's Pat Reavy notes Bundy told the St. George News he rejects licensing and registration laws, and recalls his 2016 occupation of Oregon's Malheur National Wildlife Refuge.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: University of Utah investigating report of assault, racist language and threats
item.description: University of Utah police are investigating an assault reported Thursday night near Stillwell Field in Fort Douglas, in which a group of teenagers allegedly shouted anti-Asian slurs at a student before one of them punched the student in the face. According to a campus alert, two students living in university housing were crossing Fort Douglas Boulevard when a white sedan passed, turned around and let out five or six boys estimated to be 15 or 16, who surrounded one of them. Both students got away and the teens left. KSL's Joe R. Wirthlin Jr. reports the university condemned the attack and asked anyone with information to call campus police at 801-585-2677.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Saratoga Springs father pleads guilty to federal charge, kidnapping children to Mexico
item.description: Dane Stephen Richman, 46, of Saratoga Springs pleaded guilty Sept. 30 to a federal international parental kidnapping charge after taking his two young sons to Mexico instead of returning them to their mother in May. Prosecutors said he quit his job, emptied his bank accounts and let his home go to foreclosure, then claimed he was camping in California while crossing into San Felipe, Mexico, around May 19. The children were found safe on May 26 after a statewide Amber Alert and an FBI-assisted search, and their mother received temporary sole custody. KSL's Cassidy Wixom reports the plea deal recommends time served, a year of probation, supervised visits and a mental evaluation, with sentencing set for Dec. 16; he has prior fraud and theft convictions.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Prosecutors seeking death penalty for man charged with killing mom, other man in Springville
item.description: Utah County Attorney Jeff Gray has filed notice that prosecutors will pursue the death penalty against Matthew Jacob Leonard, 28, of Springville, who faces two counts of aggravated murder in the deaths of his mother, Sarah Johnson, and John Waldron Handricks, 50, of Salt Lake City. Neither body has been found. Charging documents say witnesses heard about five gunshots at the Springville home around March 20, Leonard's phone went dark for roughly 12 hours, and he later spent 16 hours in a remote part of Duchesne County. KSL's Emily Ashcraft reports that investigators found two pools of blood, a bullet in the drywall and .22-caliber casings, and that Leonard allegedly told a new tenant in his mother's room she had probably overdosed.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Utah agriculture officials recall broccoli seeds from Spanish Fork over salmonella risk
item.description: Anyone who bought Gardeners Basics Waltham 29 Broccoli Sprouting Seeds online should stop using them, the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food said Friday, citing a possible salmonella risk. The Spanish Fork company sold the 1-pound green-and-white bags, marked "Packed for 2027" with UPC 848137042889, nationwide through Amazon, Walmart, eBay, Etsy, TikTok Shop and its own website, and sales stopped Thursday; no store purchases are affected. Department spokesman Leon Page said the seeds and anything sprouted from them should be bagged and thrown away, and no illnesses had been reported to the FDA as of Tuesday. KSL's Joe R. Wirthlin Jr. reports Gardeners Basics is offering refunds.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Strong Panama quake damages buildings, disrupts power and air travel
item.description: A magnitude 7.7 earthquake centered near La Pitaloza in Panama's rural Herrera province struck Friday at a shallow depth of about 7.8 miles, cracking homes, collapsing buildings in Penonome and setting off more than a dozen aftershocks. Power failed in six provinces, Tocumen International Airport halted flights, Panama City's Metro stopped, and classes were canceled nationwide, though the Panama Canal kept operating and a brief tsunami threat passed. Nestor Luque of Panama's geosciences institute attributed the quake to built-up stress on the Azuero Sona fault system, and the USGS warned of possible casualties and losses of 1% to 10% of GDP. Reuters' Elida Moreno reports the shaking reached Costa Rica's capital, days before a planned national evacuation drill.
item.dc:creator: Elida Moreno, Reuters

item.title: 'Deeply disturbing': Utah leaders react to plans for public execution of Fort Hood shooter
item.description: Utah leaders criticized Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's plan to livestream the Dec. 3 firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist convicted in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting that killed 13. Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson called it deeply disturbing, Gov. Spencer Cox shared a post calling it barbaric, and Sen. John Curtis cited the Stoic philosopher Seneca in urging Hegseth to reconsider, though he said questions about regretting his confirmation vote were irrelevant. Sen. Mike Lee's office did not respond; he previously called for a public execution of Tyler Robinson. KSL's Bridger Beal-Cvetko notes bipartisan objections from Sens. Thom Tillis and Chris Murphy, while Vice President JD Vance doubted it would happen.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Have You Seen This? 'Ogden Skeleton Man' poses latest creation as Amazon driver
item.description: Ron Pippin, an Ogden resident known locally as the Ogden Skeleton Man, has spent six Octobers rearranging a collection of more than 40 skeletons on his east bench lawn into new scenes almost every day. Thursday's tableau, timed just after Amazon Prime Days, showed a skeleton delivery driver fleeing a pack of skeleton dogs with packages strewn across the grass, and a real Amazon driver stopped to pose with it. Pippin said he started the displays out of boredom during COVID-19 lockdowns, reasoning that neighbors could use cheering up too, and his collection now includes a 10-foot giant and many animal skeletons. KSL's Joe R. Wirthlin Jr. reports the scenes change daily at 2579 Fillmore Avenue and are shared online.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Katie Zacharia picked as White House press secretary
item.description: Katie Zacharia, a senior communications adviser at Trump Media & Technology Group and its Truth Social platform, has been offered the White House press secretary job left open when Karoline Leavitt departed in August, a White House official said Friday. The New York Times first reported the pick, and Zacharia did not immediately comment. An attorney and frequent Fox News and Newsmax guest, she previously spent a short stint as a Homeland Security spokesperson and was a legal adviser to Fix California, a group founded by Richard Grenell. Reuters' Jasper Ward notes she would take the podium weeks before the midterms, as a Reuters/Ipsos poll puts President Donald Trump's approval at a career-low 32%.
item.dc:creator: Jasper Ward, Reuters

item.title: Utah-based Crumbl closes dozens of locations as inflationary pressure takes a bite out of sales
item.description: Lindon-based cookie chain Crumbl is shutting 57 stores and cutting jobs at headquarters after August sales came in 70% below the level of two years earlier, according to Restaurant Business. CEO Jason McGowan reportedly took personal blame in remarks to franchise owners. Zions Bank senior economist Robert Spendlove said shoppers worried about inflation are cutting back on treats, and suggested Crumbl's costly expansion into dirty sodas shows the risk of straying from a core product when consumers tighten budgets. KSL's Heather Peterson reports the company still operates around 1,000 locations nationwide.
item.dc:creator: Heather Peterson, KSL

item.title: Russian strikes across Ukraine kill 3 people as Kyiv struggles to counter escalating attacks
item.description: Russian attacks killed three people Friday in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia, Ivano-Frankivsk and Kyiv regions, adding to a toll of more than 50 dead over three days that included 30 killed when a guided bomb hit buses and 22 killed by a missile in Pryluky. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that strikes on the power grid and other infrastructure will likely intensify before winter and pressed NATO allies for Patriot ammunition and interceptors, while Kyiv reopened heated public help stations in hard-hit districts. Ukraine struck back with drones that damaged a Yandex data center in Russia's Kaluga region and targeted a refinery in Ukhta, and Russia said it shot down 505 drones overnight. The Associated Press's Hanna Arhirova and Katie Marie Davies report two people were killed in Russia's Belgorod region.
item.dc:creator: Hanna Arhirova and Katie Marie Davies, Associated Press

item.title: Lightsaber Darth Vader used in 'I am your father' duel in 'Empire Strikes Back' is up for auction
item.description: Heritage Auctions expects at least $1 million for a Darth Vader lightsaber prop used in the Cloud City fight of "The Empire Strikes Back," the scene containing the "I am your father" reveal, and again in "Return of the Jedi." It headlines a Nov. 12 sale of "Star Wars" memorabilia spanning all nine episodes plus spinoff films and series, with more than two dozen lightsabers on offer. Other lots include Boba Fett's blaster, a Yoda puppet hand operated by Frank Oz, a signed early script owned by C-3PO actor Anthony Daniels and a "Rogue One" TIE pilot helmet. The Associated Press notes the auction follows the record $3.75 million paid in July for Luke Skywalker's lightsaber, complete with severed hand, from the same duel.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Utah County man allegedly detains 'doorbell ditchers' with Taser
item.description: Police say a 55-year-old Saratoga Springs man followed a group of teens he caught ringing doorbells and running, then held them in a yard by repeatedly sparking a Taser while ordering them to call their parents. Tyson Dean Powers was booked Thursday into the Utah County Jail for investigation of four counts of aggravated kidnapping involving two 14-year-olds and two 15-year-olds. The Taser never touched any of the teens, and the standoff ended after a neighbor told the man to go home, according to the booking affidavit. KSL's Pat Reavy reports the arresting officer asked that Powers be held without bail, citing his job as a Delta Air Lines pilot as a flight risk.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: ICE says it values its accord with Utah police department in wake of chief's critical comments
item.description: The Department of Homeland Security defended a Sept. 30 operation in which ICE agents rode along with North Valley Police officers in Sanpete County and detained five immigrants, saying all had criminal histories such as repeated illegal reentry and DUI-related offenses. The statement responded to Police Chief Steve Gray, who said earlier in the week that some agents' tactics clashed with his department's values and that he is reconsidering its 287(g) cooperation agreement. DHS said it values the partnership, praised its officers' professionalism, and argued that departments refusing cooperation force a more visible federal presence, though it did not say whether the charges were convictions. KSL's Tim Vandenack notes 11 Utah sheriff's offices and three police departments, including North Valley, hold such agreements.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: TeamSmile brings free dental care to children at America First Field
item.description: The nonprofit TeamSmile turned America First Field in Sandy into a free pediatric dental clinic on Friday, with volunteer dentists and hygienists providing cleanings and fillings. Executive director John McCarthy said the group teams up with pro sports franchises across several leagues and invites children from Title I schools and others with many students on free or reduced-price lunch. Clinical director Megan Shepard said players, mascots and music help ease kids' nerves, and the group also connects patients with dentists for follow-up treatment. KSL's Madi Vollmer reports TeamSmile says it has delivered more than $25 million in care to over 70,000 children and is recruiting local volunteers.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Isaias strengthens into a dangerous Category 3 hurricane on track toward the Gulf Coast
item.description: Hurricane Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, grew into a Category 3 storm with 120 mph winds Friday as it approached a landfall expected that evening between Alabama's Mobile Bay and Florida's Choctawhatchee Bay. The National Hurricane Center warned of storm surge up to 9 feet, tornadoes and 4 to 8 inches of rain across southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and southwest Georgia, with some spots seeing up to 15 inches. Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey ordered non-residents out of Gulf Shores, Orange Beach and Dauphin Island, and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said about 5,000 Guard troops would mobilize. The Associated Press's Dave Collins and Gerald Herbert report the storm should weaken to a tropical storm inland by Saturday, while Hurricane Simon was strengthening in the Pacific.
item.dc:creator: Dave Collins and Gerald Herbert, Associated Press

item.title: Almost all Gaza residents need shelter as El Niño threatens flooding, UN agency says
item.description: The International Organization for Migration warned Friday that nearly all of Gaza's roughly 2 million residents need tents or shelter help before winter, as a potentially record-strength El Niño threatens heavy rain and flooding. IOM Director General Amy Pope said only about 17% of winter shelter needs have been met, blaming Israeli limits on aid; the agency says about 8,600 shelter kits have been blocked as dual-use items. More than half of existing tents need replacing, some 3,600 buildings were flagged in August as at risk of collapse, and about 1.8 million people live in displacement sites, many prone to flooding. Reuters' Olivia Le Poidevin reports that COGAT, the Israeli military body overseeing aid, did not immediately comment.
item.dc:creator: Olivia Le Poidevin, Reuters

item.title: Former ICC Judge Navi Pillay wins 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
item.description: The Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay, an 85-year-old South African jurist who has served on the International Criminal Court and the Rwanda tribunal and led a U.N. inquiry that found Israel committed genocide in Gaza. The committee framed the honor as a defense of international law under strain, and it came the same day the United States sanctioned the ICC itself; Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office denounced the choice. Pillay, a former U.N. human rights chief and the first non-white woman on South Africa's High Court, learned of the award at a conference in Nuremberg and dedicated it to survivors of international crimes. Reuters reports the roughly $1.2 million prize will be presented in Oslo on Dec. 10.
item.dc:creator: Gwladys Fouche, Nora Buli and Christine Uyanik, Reuters

item.title: Delta warns of more airline capacity restraint as fuel shock hits profits
item.description: Delta Air Lines trimmed its 2026 adjusted earnings forecast to $5.10 to $5.60 a share, down from $6.50 to $7.50, after projecting its fuel bill will climb about $6 billion this year as the Iran war pushes jet fuel prices higher. CEO Ed Bastian said the airline has raised fares roughly 20% with little pushback but argued the industry must hold back on adding flights next year, because growth will not offset high costs. Third-quarter profit of $1.72 a share fell slightly short of estimates, and airline stocks slipped Friday, though Delta's Philadelphia-area refinery is expected to save it more than $700 million this year. Reuters' Rajesh Kumar Singh and Shivansh Tiwary report Delta expects strong premium and corporate demand to lift fourth-quarter revenue about 20%.
item.dc:creator: Rajesh Kumar Singh and Shivansh Tiwary, Reuters

item.title: FBI arrests suspect in ShinyHunters hack of the bureau's jobs portal
item.description: FBI Director Kash Patel announced Friday the arrest of an alleged co-conspirator in ShinyHunters, the hacking group that claimed it stole personal data on nearly every FBI employee through the bureau's jobs portal. Patel said the breach happened on a platform run by an outside vendor and vowed to dismantle the rest of the group, though the suspect's name and charges were not released. ShinyHunters had cast the hack as retaliation for a May FBI advisory describing it as an extortion-focused data-breach crew. The Associated Press's Eric Tucker reports experts see national security risks because exposed agents and their spouses could face extortion or swatting.
item.dc:creator: Eric Tucker, Associated Press

item.title: New documentary asks, 'Is this Joseph Smith?'
item.description: "Brother Joseph Again," an independent documentary examining whether an 1840s daguerreotype shows Latter-day Saint founder Joseph Smith, opened in Utah theaters Friday after a premiere at Jordan Commons in Sandy. The image sits in a locket that Smith descendant Daniel Larsen inherited in 1992 but did not open until 2020. Producers Joseph Brickey, a forensic artist, and historian Patrick Bishop spent four years comparing the face with Smith's death mask and a reconstructed skull, aided by Community of Christ archivists. KSL's Carole Mikita notes that The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, which received the locket as a donation, has said it cannot determine who is pictured.
item.dc:creator: Carole Mikita, KSL

item.title: Hundreds join in 'final walk' at hospital with 20-year-old Lehi man who died tragically
item.description: Hundreds of people dressed in blue, his favorite color, lined a hospital hallway Tuesday for an honor walk as 20-year-old Lehi resident Dominic Millward was taken to donate his organs. His mother, Mary Millward, said he and two friends drank an unidentified substance from an unmarked bottle that they believed was a sleep aid; another young man died and a third survived, and investigators have not yet identified the drink. She described her son, the oldest of six children, as a self-taught mechanic who loved restoring cars and had recently found a business opportunity and a girlfriend on a trip to Japan. The family has set up the DomWorthy fund to help people who are struggling, KSL's Arianne Brown reports, and he will be buried in Idaho.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Fighting fire with fire
item.description: Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, toured a U.S. Forest Service prescribed burn near Richfield on Wednesday, his first time seeing one in person, days after urging Senate passage of the Wildfire Emissions Prevention Act to ease regulatory barriers to controlled burns. Richfield District Ranger Jason Kling told the Deseret News that last year's Monroe Canyon fire cost about $1,500 an acre to suppress, compared with under $40 an acre for the planned burn. Fishlake National Forest supervisor Mike Elson said fire cannot be removed from these landscapes, so crews choose to burn under controlled conditions in spring and fall after months of planning. Reporter Emily Walker describes the 21-element burn plans and the ignition tools crews use, from helicopter-slung helitorches to drones dropping chemical spheres.
item.dc:creator: Emily Walker, Deseret News

item.title: 4 astronauts return to Earth after 8 months in space
item.description: Four crew members came home from the International Space Station on Thursday, splashing down in a SpaceX capsule in the Pacific near Los Angeles after roughly eight months in orbit. NASA's Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, France's Sophie Adenot and Russia's Andrey Fedyaev launched in February as replacements after NASA's first-ever medical evacuation sent the previous crew home early, and their own return slipped three weeks while the relief crew's capsule was repaired. During the mission they completed seven spacewalks between Meir and Adenot, watched the Artemis II lunar flyby and marked the U.S. 250th anniversary, with Meir playing piccolo for a Boston Pops concert. The Associated Press's Marcia Dunn reports seven astronauts remain aboard the station.
item.dc:creator: Marcia Dunn, Associated Press

item.title: A 'wish list' for Ryan Smith
item.description: KSL asked people in downtown Salt Lake City what they'd want from Ryan Smith, the sports and business figure behind much of the area's redevelopment. Breakfast came up again and again: residents said downtown lacks a real bagel shop or a standout breakfast sandwich. Others wanted more live music venues and a late-night hangout that isn't built around alcohol. One resident made a specific pitch for the dumpling chain Din Tai Fung. Many said they already like downtown's restaurants and trusted Smith to deliver, pointing to the new food vendors at the Delta Center as proof that his projects tend to succeed.
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen, KSL

item.title: Amazon launches first Android tablets, raising prices and incorporating Alexa
item.description: Amazon has introduced a premium line of Alexa Tablets that run Google's Android instead of its own Fire OS, with aluminum cases and prices from $230 up to $550 for the top 128 GB model. That puts them against Apple's iPad and Samsung's Galaxy tablets, a break from the strategy of selling cheap devices to pull customers into Prime services that devices chief Panos Panay is now steering away from. The AI-powered Alexa+ assistant is built in but requires a Prime membership or a subscription. Amazon is launching the line as the tablet market shrinks: IDC data shows global sales down 12% last quarter and Amazon's own share falling to 1.9%. Removing lock-screen ads costs a one-time $20 on all but the top model, and Amazon didn't say how long it will keep supporting older Fire OS tablets.
item.dc:creator: Greg Bensinger, Reuters

item.title: Pentagon says the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed
item.description: The Pentagon said Thursday that the Dec. 3 firing-squad execution at Fort Hood of Nidal Malik Hasan, the Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people there in 2009, will be livestreamed, following Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's remark that it would be public. It would be the first U.S. military execution since 1961. Legal scholars disagreed: Fordham's Deborah Denno said livestreaming could add transparency, while Berkeley's Elisabeth Semel questioned the government's motives and the condemned man's dignity. Experts said a habeas petition in civilian court could delay the execution for years, though Hasan's trial conduct suggested he wanted a death sentence. Attorney John Galligan said Hasan was notified without a lawyer present, which he called a violation of Army rules; the Army said it made reasonable efforts to reach counsel.
item.dc:creator: Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press

item.title: Judge orders release of immigrant detained in controversial arrest as Ogden officer looked on
item.description: A Venezuelan asylum seeker whose Aug. 25 arrest by an ICE agent became a flashpoint in Ogden has been released from the Adelanto detention center in California after a federal judge granted a habeas petition Wednesday, his lawyer Sergio Garcia said. The arrest drew attention because an Ogden police officer at the scene on an unrelated dog call ended up as a go-between, and City Councilman Kevin Lundell filmed part of it. The episode prompted a heated council debate and talk from Mayor Ben Nadolski about revising police policy. The man arrived in 2022 and had a work permit while his asylum claim was pending, but he now faces deportation proceedings and must argue for asylum in immigration court. Federal officials, who say he was in the country illegally, did not respond to a request for comment.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: SpaceX takes aim at US wireless carriers with spectrum acquisition
item.description: SpaceX has agreed to buy Grain Management's nationwide 800 MHz spectrum, which Grain acquired from T-Mobile earlier this year; terms weren't disclosed. Low-band airwaves like these travel farther, get through walls and trees, and already work with most existing handsets, addressing a longtime weakness of satellite-to-phone service. Paired with SpaceX's 2 GHz holdings, the spectrum lets Starlink Mobile compete with traditional carriers rather than just filling dead zones. T-Mobile, Verizon and AT&T shares fell about 6% after hours, while Verizon's Rich Young countered that spectrum is worthless without a network to use it. The deal needs FCC approval, though Chair Brendan Carr welcomed it, and the agency approved SpaceX's plan for 15,000 next-generation satellites the same week.
item.dc:creator: Akash Sriram and David Shepardson, Reuters

item.title: Hunters in southern Utah can help protect California condors and maybe win a prize
item.description: Lead poisoning is still the top killer of wild California condors in Utah and Arizona, because the birds scavenge gut piles and carcasses left by hunters. Through its Hunters Helping Condors program, the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources is asking Zion unit hunters to switch to lead-free ammunition or carry animal remains out of the field. Permit holders can get a coupon for free non-lead ammunition, which the agency says is in short supply, so hunters should redeem it soon. Hunters who show proof of using lead-free rounds at a check station can enter a drawing for an $800 outdoor-gear gift card.
item.dc:creator: KSL Staff

item.title: Ogden man who manipulated teen into sending explicit photos given 10 years in prison
item.description: Tyler Justin Pitt, a 28-year-old Ogden man, was sentenced Wednesday in federal court in St. George to 10 years in prison followed by lifetime supervision. Pitt had pleaded guilty in February to coercion and enticement and to receiving child sexual abuse material; a production charge was dismissed. Prosecutors said he met a southern Utah girl on Snapchat in late 2023, persuaded her they were in an exclusive relationship even though he lived with a girlfriend, and pressured her for about six months to send explicit images, until her mother found out in 2024. A search of his devices turned up exchanges with other girls and women and 22 unrelated abuse images. Prosecutors had asked Judge Ann Marie McIff Allen for 12.5 years, arguing the evidence showed a broader pattern.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: The Trump administration is suspending Microsoft from a green card program, alleging fraud
item.description: Vice President JD Vance announced Thursday that Microsoft is being suspended from the labor-certification process companies use to sponsor H-1B workers for green cards, accusing it of fraud by running token job ads to claim no Americans applied. He said Microsoft laid off 6,000 U.S. workers last year while securing 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards; the company did not immediately respond. Doug Rand, a former Biden administration official, called the move incoherent, arguing that green cards free workers from dependence on their employers. Officials also named nine universities, including Harvard, Stanford and MIT, for possible J-1 visa abuse. The announcement came hours before Trump was due to give Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.
item.dc:creator: Seung Min Kim, Rebecca Santana and Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press

item.title: Watch live: 4th Congressional District candidates make their case on debate stage
item.description: This preview post carried a livestream of Thursday night's debate in Utah's newly drawn 4th Congressional District, with fewer than four weeks until Election Day. Republican Rep. Mike Kennedy, a former longtime state legislator now in his first House term, is running in the new district after a judge redrew Utah's congressional map last year. His Democratic opponent, Marine veteran Jonny Larsen, served two Iraq deployments and is making his first run for Congress. The debate was set for 6 p.m. at Snow College's Eccles Performing Arts Center in Ephraim, moderated by Deseret News executive editor Doug Wilks. It is the third of four congressional debates the Utah Debate Commission is hosting this fall.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Trump administration wants universities to pay fees for international students
item.description: The Department of Homeland Security has proposed making colleges pay $70,000 for each international student they recommend for Optional Practical Training, which lets F-1 visa holders work in their field, plus $30,000 for each renewal. DHS calls the program a channel for cheap foreign labor and says the fees, payable to the Treasury, would make schools screen candidates more carefully; public comments are open through Nov. 9. Randy McCrillis, the University of Utah's vice provost for global engagement, said the fees would be an insurmountable barrier for schools; 918 U. students currently use the program. NAFSA chief Fanta Aw warned that driving away international students would hurt American innovation. The proposal adds to a string of Trump administration moves against foreign students, including visa revocations and a four-year stay limit that a court has blocked.
item.dc:creator: Jason Swensen, Deseret News

item.title: Starbucks declines comment on Chipotle takeover report, says laser focused on turnaround
item.description: Starbucks declined to comment on a Financial Times report that it had worked with advisers on a possible takeover of Chipotle. The company said it remains focused on the turnaround led by CEO Brian Niccol, who ran Chipotle for about six years before moving to Starbucks in 2024. Chipotle shares jumped 6% on the news, valuing the chain at about $41 billion, while Starbucks closed roughly flat. RBC's Logan Reich and other analysts questioned the strategic logic and warned a deal could require heavy borrowing mid-overhaul, though some said Starbucks' licensed partners in Europe could speed Chipotle's expansion abroad. Starbucks has had four straight quarters of comparable sales growth, but its adjusted operating margin has fallen to 14.4%.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: New Box Elder County sheriff to be elected as three remaining candidates vie for the office
item.description: Box Elder County voters will choose a new sheriff after deputy Mike Allred beat incumbent Kevin Potter in the June Republican primary; Allred now faces independents Doug Christensen and Allen Shinney, after a third, Chad Hayman, stopped campaigning. All three were shaped by a January dispute in which three cities moved their emergency dispatch to Weber Area 911. Allred, a six-year deputy who was injured alongside his K-9 in the 2025 shooting that killed two Tremonton-Garland officers, says he is repairing the relationship with the state-run dispatch center. Christensen, a 16-year Utah Highway Patrol trooper from Bear River City, wants deputies more involved in communities and with young people. Shinney, a retired former Utah State Tax Commission enforcement director, says he saved taxpayers $10 million and has no local political ties.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Lindon woman celebrates 99th birthday by sharing her lifelong love of music
item.description: Dottie Beaver spent her 99th birthday on Thursday the way she spends many days at Spring Gardens Senior Living in Lindon: playing the piano while other residents gather to listen. She studied music in college and still remembers the hour a day she spent practicing in a room with nothing but a piano. Neighbors like Lowell Nelson say her playing first drew them in. Her daughter, Terri Hanson, said performing is what makes her mother happiest. Beaver, who wore a crown and sash for the occasion, calls her musical talent a gift from God.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: Utah man creates app to combat porn addiction through accountability
item.description: Provo entrepreneur Tyler Patterson built the Ever Accountable app around the idea that being accountable to another person works better than content blocking for breaking a pornography habit. The app uses AI to watch the user's screen, including social media feeds, and reports explicit or borderline material to a chosen partner, such as a spouse. Patterson says 95% of users quickly cut their porn use. The app requires an annual subscription, and Patterson said part of the revenue pays to give it free to people who can't afford it. He argues that the habit depends on secrecy and that people start to recover once they talk openly about it.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: RFK Jr. tasks researchers with studying vaccine injuries
item.description: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has launched a vaccine injury research center at the National Institutes of Health and proposed changes to the federal adverse-event reporting system, including paying doctors who report suspected injuries. Kennedy, who previewed the plan in a September speech to the anti-vaccine group he co-founded, says vaccine harms have gone unstudied, while the CDC describes serious reactions as very rare. Vaccine scientists Peter Hotez and Paul Offit said existing surveillance already caught extremely rare COVID-vaccine side effects. They warned that the center could be used to confirm Kennedy's existing beliefs. The move comes as vaccination rates fall and Pennsylvania deals with the country's worst measles outbreak in decades, with more than 1,000 cases and five deaths, all in unvaccinated people.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Owermohle, Meg Tirrell and Deidre McPhillips, CNN

item.title: 'Not just a vehicle': Utah food truck launches fundraiser to get back to business after accident
item.description: Fatty Tuna Sushi and Ramen, a family food truck that has operated in Utah for about a decade, is running a GoFundMe after a Sept. 18 crash took the truck off the road. The heavily loaded truck couldn't stop in time on southbound I-15 near Lindon and rear-ended another vehicle; no one was hurt, but the front end and windshield were damaged and the kitchen equipment inside shifted. Owner Marc Tien said the truck carries only liability insurance, so towing, repairs, equipment checks and lost income all fall on the family, and parts for the older vehicle are hard to find. Meanwhile, the business is working from a trailer rented from another vendor, with a smaller menu. The fundraiser had brought in a little more than $6,000 as of Thursday.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Tooele County Planning Commission votes to table draft of data center ordinance
item.description: After a crowded meeting that ran past 11 p.m. Wednesday, the Tooele County Planning Commission voted unanimously to shelve the sixth draft of Chapter 34, its proposed rules for data centers, along with related land use amendments. Vice-chair Toni Scott's motion puts the chapter on hold until the board settles what counts as a data center and answers questions left over from earlier delays. Alternate member Richard Mitchell, an aerospace engineer, said he wouldn't support any changes until the ordinance was fixed, and members of the group TooeleCARES read a letter signed by more than 900 residents. Assistant county manager Brittany Lopez said the county won't take data center applications until the chapter is done, though at least one developer has expressed interest. The commission meets next on Oct. 28.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Utah mom's breast cancer diagnosis highlights importance of screening
item.description: Intermountain Health employee Dani Kurtz, a former labor and delivery nurse, is urging women not to put off screenings and to pay attention to changes in their bodies. In January 2025 she felt a lump in her armpit even though her mammogram came back normal, likely because dense breast tissue can hide tumors; with her mother recently diagnosed, she pushed for an ultrasound and MRI, which found seven tumors. She had a double mastectomy, 16 rounds of chemotherapy and radiation, and finished treatment late last year. State data shows only about 63.8% of Utah women 40 and older had a mammogram in the past two years, against a goal of 81% by 2030. Dr. Jonathan Shakespear of Intermountain's Breast Care Center said screening late is better than not at all, and pointed to a new online tool for finding the soonest available appointment nearby.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: Rubio says US pressure on NATO allies to boost defense spending is 'not hostile'
item.description: Speaking in Lisbon at the end of a tour of Iceland, Greece and Portugal, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington's push for NATO allies to spend more on defense should not be read as hostility, while acknowledging that smaller members struggle to pay for big projects. He warned that a deadlocked war in Ukraine could spread through Russian sabotage in neighboring NATO states. Rubio said the U.S. will keep pursuing a negotiated settlement but won't put effort into talks that go nowhere. Portugal spends just over 2% of GDP on defense and plans to reach about 3%, still below Trump's 5% demand. Its decision to let U.S. forces use Lajes Field in the Azores during the Iran war is now being reviewed by the attorney general after a Left Bloc complaint.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Lee and Barry Hatton, Associated Press

item.title: Convicted sex offender accused of downloading pornography at Salt Lake library
item.description: Adrian Mathias Perea, 55, who is already on federal supervised release for a 2020 child pornography conviction, was charged Thursday in 3rd District Court with nine second-degree felony counts of sexual exploitation of a minor, each with a habitual sex offender enhancement. Investigators say they traced peer-to-peer downloads of abuse material to the Salt Lake City Library in September. When they confronted Perea there on Tuesday, the same file-sharing software was open on his laptop, and charging documents estimate thousands of illicit files on the computer. After first denying it, Perea admitted to downloading the material at the library for several months, the charges say. His listed address is the homeless shelter in South Salt Lake.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Zion to reopen highway section more than week after rockfall cleanup
item.description: Drivers will be able to go straight from Zion Canyon to the park's east entrance again at 9 a.m. Friday, ending the need for the U.S. 89 detour. Park officials had warned the Zion-Mt. Carmel Highway could stay shut for weeks after a major rockfall damaged it on Sept. 30. Instead, crews used a stopgap: they removed the broken asphalt and laid gravel, with proper repaving to come later. The last stretch to reopen runs 2.5 miles from Great Arch Pullout to Canyon Junction, after a 7.5-mile segment on the Kane County side reopened Tuesday. The park is asking motorists to watch for workers and pedestrians in the construction zone.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Taliban firmly in control in Afghanistan 25 years after US-led invasion to oust them
item.description: Twenty-five years after the U.S.-led invasion of Oct. 7, 2001, and five years after the chaotic American withdrawal, the Taliban are back in firm control of Afghanistan. Afghans interviewed by the AP described the two decades of U.S. presence as bringing real gains for media and women, alongside corruption and resentment. Security has improved since 2021, but women and girls are again barred from secondary and higher education and most work, a loss that obstetrician Nigar Nangrahari said new roads and buildings can't make up for. Tahmina Mangal, who now runs a clothing shop after her studies were cut off, urged women to keep learning online. Deputy government spokesman Hamdullah Fitrat called the anniversary a dark day and said Afghans will never accept foreign occupation.
item.dc:creator: Elena Becatoros and Abdul Qahar Afghan, Associated Press

item.title: Drunk driver crashes into downtown Salt Lake City concert venue, police say
item.description: No patrons or staff were inside The State Room on State Street when a vehicle rolled into its front around 1:40 a.m. Thursday after a two-car collision outside, police said. The crash broke the venue's front windows, damaged its facade and bent the metal fencing in front. Salt Lake City police said one injured driver was cited for DUI, but didn't say whether anyone else was hurt or whether there were passengers. The venue said it is grateful nobody was seriously injured and is working to reopen in time for this weekend's shows, though it asked fans to be patient if plans change.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: USA Climbing hosts final boulder event of 2026 World Climbing Series in Utah
item.description: Salt Lake City's Smith's Ballpark will host the last bouldering stop of the 2026 World Climbing Series from Oct. 16 to 18. The field includes Paris 2024 Olympians such as Colorado climbers Brooke Raboutou and Collin Duffy. Men's and women's qualifying rounds are on Friday, with the men's finals Saturday and the women's finals closing the event Sunday. In bouldering, climbers go without ropes or harnesses on a roughly 4.5-meter wall over safety mats. Under USA Climbing's rules, a problem counts as complete when the climber holds the top hold with both hands under control.
item.dc:creator: KSL Staff

item.title: Remnants of Hurricane Rachel head to Utah. How much water will it provide?
item.description: What is left of Hurricane Rachel, which peaked as a Category 2 storm off Mexico, is expected to merge over Utah this weekend with a low-pressure system dropping down from Alaska, bringing several days of heavy rain from Saturday into midweek. KSL Weather models show three or more inches possible in the mountains and 1.5 to 2 inches in cities such as St. George, Salt Lake City and Logan, though shadowed spots like Fillmore may get less. National Weather Service meteorologist Hayden Mahan said Sunday and Monday carry the highest flooding risk for slot canyons, dry washes, burn scars and urban areas. Even so, forecasters say the timing helps, since more than 75% of Utah is still in severe or extreme drought. The rain won't do much for reservoirs, but wetter soil should make next spring's snowmelt runoff more efficient.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Private plane makes emergency landing inside Hill Air Force Base
item.description: A pilot flying alone walked away uninjured after setting a civilian plane down inside Hill Air Force Base on Thursday morning, base officials said. The plane had reportedly developed engine trouble and came down near Wardleigh and Perimeter roads by the north gate. The base temporarily closed that gate while its emergency crews responded. Hill safety staff are working with the Federal Aviation Administration to find out what went wrong and to figure out how to get the aircraft off the base.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: The Waffle House Index helps Southerners — and FEMA — gauge a storm's severity
item.description: The informal Waffle House Index rates a storm by how well the local Waffle House is still operating: green for a full menu and little damage nearby, yellow for a limited menu probably cooked on generator power, and red for a closed restaurant in a likely hard-hit area. Former FEMA administrator Craig Fugate says he came up with the idea after Hurricane Charley in 2004, when a limited-menu Waffle House was the only food he could find. He kept using color-coded maps of the restaurants at FEMA. The chain's resilience is deliberate: after Hurricane Katrina destroyed seven locations in 2005, executives saw how much business flowed to the stores that reopened quickly. Waffle House now has generators, a mobile command center, its own storm center and staff trained to cook without power across its roughly 1,900 restaurants.
item.dc:creator: Hannah Schoenbaum, Associated Press

item.title: Police find missing runaway in southern Utah, arrest mom for suspected child abuse
item.description: Erika Leyva Gutierrez, 38, of St. George, was booked early Thursday for investigation of aggravated child abuse. According to a booking affidavit, the case began when her 13-year-old son ran away, saying he had been served spoiled meat, and his older sister found him at a park. Relatives told police the mother used her children as unpaid help in her food business and threatened not to feed them unless they paid for their own food or brought home enough money. The sister also said their mother had threatened to kill the boy that day, and family members said they had recorded some of the threats. Gutierrez denied the allegations when questioned.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Trump signs disaster order unlocking federal aid for 2 Utah counties affected by fire, flooding
item.description: A federal disaster declaration signed by President Trump on Thursday lets FEMA cover up to 75% of eligible infrastructure repairs in Beaver and Piute counties, where state officials estimate at least $47 million in qualifying damage. The losses come from the Cottonwood Fire, which burned more than 97,400 acres starting June 22 and damaged structures including much of Eagle Point Resort. July monsoon debris flows across the burn scar then affected about 200 Beaver homes, wrecked Beaver City Power's hydroelectric system, fouled water supplies and closed roads such as state Route 153, parts of which may stay shut until next year. Gov. Spencer Cox called it a one-two punch that the rural communities couldn't afford to fix alone. This is Utah's first major disaster declaration since the 2023 floods, in what has been the state's second-worst fire year by acreage.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Don't miss the Draconid meteor shower, a celestial event that won't take all night
item.description: The Draconid meteor shower is best seen in the early evening rather than before dawn, with a forecast peak of about 7 p.m. MDT Thursday, according to EarthSky. Northern Hemisphere viewers have the best view, and the thin waning moon shouldn't wash out the roughly 10 slow-moving meteors an hour, each visible for a second or two. The debris comes from comet 21P/Giacobini-Zinner, which circles the sun about every seven years. Because the comet has passed fairly close to Earth recently, a sudden outburst or even a meteor storm is possible. No equipment is needed: find a dark spot away from city lights, lie back and watch the northern sky near Draco.
item.dc:creator: Ashley Strickland, CNN

item.title: University of Utah gets $7.5M federal grant to advance domestic critical minerals search
item.description: A University of Utah-led consortium will receive $7.5 million from the Department of Energy to look for critical minerals and rare earth elements in unconventional places such as coal seams and mining and industrial waste; outside funding brings the total to nearly $10 million. The project is one of six regional efforts in DOE's Carbon Ore, Rare Earth and Critical Minerals Initiative and widens earlier basin-level work, including a $1.5 million Uinta Basin study, to eight regions. Principal investigator Michael Free said there is an urgent need for domestic supply, and geology lead Lauren Birgenheier said the new phase will sharpen estimates of resource volumes. Partners include the University of Wyoming, the Colorado School of Mines, New Mexico Tech and several national labs. The grant fits Gov. Spencer Cox's "Mission Critical" push to reduce reliance on China, which dominates global refining of these materials.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Public input requested on Grand Canyon North Rim plans
item.description: The National Park Service is taking public comment on three draft concepts for redeveloping Grand Canyon's North Rim, one of which would provide year-round access and lodging with a larger developed area. Superintendent Ed Keable said the past year's disasters, the 2025 Dragon Bravo Fire and this year's flooding, show why careful planning matters. Melinda Rich Marshall of Jacob Lake Inn said the business lost roughly $2 million and ran at about 30% occupancy this summer, compared with about 70% in a normal year. A virtual meeting is planned along with open houses Oct. 19 in Kanab, Oct. 20 in Flagstaff and Oct. 21 in Tusayan, Andrew Adams reports.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Man who drove into police car is given second chance through recovery court
