item.description: Steven Lopez, 35, will enter Salt Lake County's recovery court under a plea in abeyance after pleading guilty to stealing a van and to aggravated assault for ramming a police vehicle in November 2025. District Attorney Sim Gill said Lopez had been asked to leave a West Valley City shelter for erratic behavior, took a van from a nearby auto shop and drove back to the shelter, where he hit an officer's unmarked car. Detective Greg Celentano fired three shots that missed, and Lopez later returned and surrendered, telling investigators he was high. If Lopez completes three years of probation and at least 15 months of recovery court, his record can be cleared, and Gill earlier declined to charge Celentano, Emily Ashcraft reports.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Margaret Hamilton, whose software helped land Apollo astronauts on the moon, has died
item.description: Margaret Hamilton, the MIT software pioneer whose team wrote the onboard code that guided NASA's Apollo missions, died Sept. 30 at 90, MIT announced. Hamilton joined MIT in 1959, ran the Instrumentation Laboratory's software division and led about 100 engineers, and she popularized the term "software engineering." NASA credits her software with keeping Apollo 11's landing on track when it handled an erroneous processing request minutes before touchdown, and one of her safeguards came from a crash her young daughter caused in a simulator. She received NASA's Exceptional Space Act Award in 2003 and the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016, Jackie Wattles of CNN reports.
item.dc:creator: Jackie Wattles, CNN

item.title: Ogden School District sees student lunch debt skyrocket, turns to community for help
item.description: Ogden School District says unpaid student meal balances have jumped about 500% to roughly $16,000, compared with about $3,000 in a typical year. Kitchen staff, including Polk Elementary's Brynne Wilson and Mount Fort Junior High's Dix Wright, link the increase to the first year of H.B. 100, which expanded free-meal eligibility and bars schools from swapping meals or confronting students over debt. Fewer families are filing federal free-lunch applications, with participation falling from about 75% to 68%, so the district absorbs costs for families who would likely qualify. The local school nutrition association is holding a $30 "Miles for Meals" fun run Saturday at Lorin Farr Park to help pay down the debt.
item.dc:creator: Brenna Donnelly, KSL

item.title: Former East Layton police officer pleads no contest to child sex abuse charges
item.description: Thomas Jackson, a 78-year-old former East Layton police officer, has pleaded no contest to five child sex abuse felonies and is serving five consecutive prison terms of 1 to 15 years, with no parole eligibility before 2030. KSL's COLD podcast reports that after an earlier 1986 conviction for abusing his daughters, Heidi Holmberg and Tori Riddle, Jackson got probation without jail time, and he was later imprisoned in Idaho for abusing stepdaughters. The current case grew out of a 2023 call, made at a detective's urging, in which Holmberg got her father to describe years of abuse. Davis County is also investigating Jackson in the 1975 disappearance of Nancy Baird, long blamed on Ted Bundy, but no remains turned up when deputies dug up his former backyard in 2025, Dave Cawley reports.
item.dc:creator: Dave Cawley, KSL

item.title: Utah County Warming Center opens Nov. 1 providing warm beds, expanded programs
item.description: Utah County's warming center will be open nightly from 8 p.m. to 8 a.m., Nov. 1 through March 15, 2027, at the county public works warehouse on State Street between Provo and Springville. Community Action Services and Food Bank runs the shelter for adults, and this season it adds a "Laying the Roots" skills program and weekly resource nights with service agencies. Commissioner Skyler Beltran pointed to the latest Point-in-Time Count, which the county says showed a drop of 45 homeless people, more than 60% of the statewide decline. Organizers credit state funding, local partners and volunteers, and about 600 people used the county's warming centers in the 2024-25 season.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ donates $3M for National Juneteenth Museum in Texas
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints will give $3 million toward the planned 50,000-square-foot National Juneteenth Museum in Fort Worth, Texas, including a FamilySearch-powered genealogy center focused on African American family records that are hard to trace. The pledge was announced Wednesday at a ceremonial demolition on the site, held on the 100th birthday of Opal Lee, the retired teacher known as the "Grandmother of Juneteenth." Lee and museum CEO Jarred Howard praised the gift, and Elder Michael A. Dunn spoke for the Church, which says the partnership grew out of Lee's 2022 visit to its headquarters. The Church also gave 38,000 pounds of food to five local food banks.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Heart transplant recipient comes home to neighborhood parade
item.description: Neighbors, police and firefighters in Plain City lined the route home for 10-year-old Brandon "Chomp" Barela, who received a heart transplant on Sept. 1. Chomp, who has Down syndrome and was born with heart defects, went into severe heart failure this summer and needed a left ventricular assist device before he was listed for a new heart. His mother, Kourtney Barela, said word of a match arrived on Aug. 30, just after a small birthday party at Primary Children's Hospital. Because Chomp must avoid close contact for months, she asked a few relatives to wave from the roadside, and the plan grew into a community parade after she posted it online.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Police link finding of human remains near Vernal to remains found in September
item.description: Uintah County deputies found skeletal remains Wednesday near Little Mountain, about 15 miles northwest of Vernal, in the same area where human remains were discovered Sept. 27. The sheriff's office said investigators believe the two finds are connected, and they recovered additional related items at the site. The state medical examiner will examine the remains, and the investigation is ongoing.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: Ryan Smith launches survey in search for 'strong local vibe' at SLC entertainment district
item.description: Smith Entertainment Group CEO Ryan Smith has launched an online survey asking Utahns which local restaurants and shops they want in the planned sports and entertainment district east of the Delta Center, much like the fan vote that named the Mammoth. The arena's renovation is two-thirds done, and construction on the district is expected to begin next year after Smith closes a $55.4 million purchase of 6.5 acres of Salt Palace land in early 2027. Plans so far include a 6,000-seat Live Nation concert venue, a hotel, possible housing towers and a promenade over a lowered 300 West, paid for in part by a 0.5% city sales tax. Meanwhile, the Salt Palace will close entirely for three years starting in fall 2027 as part of a $1.8 billion downtown overhaul, Carter Williams reports.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Samsung flags $80 billion profit on AI boom, highest quarterly for any tech company
item.description: Samsung Electronics expects third-quarter operating profit of about 107.4 trillion won, or $80 billion, nearly nine times last year's figure and the first time any tech company has topped 100 trillion won in a quarter. It is Samsung's fourth straight record quarter, driven by AI-related demand for DRAM, NAND and high-bandwidth memory that has outrun supply and pushed prices up, with revenue expected to rise 127%. Analysts expect the memory shortage to last into 2027-28, though higher component costs are squeezing Samsung's phone and electronics businesses and its foundry unit is still losing money. Chinese competitors and possible U.S. chip tariffs are longer-term risks, and full results are due Oct. 29, Reuters reports.
item.dc:creator: Heekyong Yang and Hyunjoo Jin, Reuters

item.title: Sandy teen who 'couldn't take it anymore' accused of killing father after years of abuse
item.description: A 15-year-old Sandy boy has been charged with manslaughter in juvenile court in the Sept. 27 shooting death of his father at the family's home near 9700 S. 1200 East. The bullet also hit his younger brother in the knee. According to charging documents, the younger boy told detectives their father had abused them for years, including a beating over his blood sugar and forcing him to take a near-lethal insulin dose for his diabetes. Both brothers told investigators the father started yelling at and hitting the younger boy that morning after their mother left for work, and the older teen said he then got his father's gun. KSL is not naming the teen, Pat Reavy reports.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Some guardrails on ChatGPT for Teens don't work as promised, watchdog group says
item.description: A Common Sense Media report says several safeguards in OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens don't work as advertised and calls the product an "unacceptable risk," urging OpenAI to limit the chatbot to adults until it is safer. The group found the chatbot did refuse explicit sexual role-play, but parent alerts for suicide, self-harm and eating-disorder risk failed, and the bot still talked like a friend despite OpenAI's promise that it would not imply it has feelings. OpenAI said much of the testing appears to predate full activation of parental controls. Common Sense Media receives funding from OpenAI and other tech companies, AP's Barbara Ortutay notes.
item.dc:creator: Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press

item.title: Department of Energy awards funding to Utah geothermal projects
item.description: Five of the 21 geothermal projects sharing $99 million in new U.S. Department of Energy grants involve Utah. Salt Lake City-based Zanskar Geothermal and Minerals, AlterG Resources and the University of Utah will test enhanced geothermal systems at sites in Nevada and New Mexico. The university and Zanskar also received exploration-drilling awards, including a University of Utah study of a large heat anomaly in the Cove Fort field, and Nevada's Raser Power Systems will look at expanding generation at a plant in the Escalante Desert. Data from the projects will go into a public federal repository, Alixel Cabrera of Utah News Dispatch reports.
item.dc:creator: Alixel Cabrera, Utah News Dispatch

item.title: Henefer baseball coach honored for saving boy from cardiac arrest
item.description: The North Summit Fire District has honored Henefer youth baseball coach Gene Richins, whose quick CPR saved 8-year-old Tyce Gardner after a thrown ball hit the boy in the chest at practice and stopped his heart. Richins began compressions while Tyce's father, Bryce, called 911, and crews from Henefer's new fire station, about half a mile from the field, arrived within minutes and restored his heartbeat with a defibrillator. Tyce was flown to Primary Children's Hospital, and doctors expect a full recovery after two days of care and a month on a heart monitor. Medical director Austin Smith praised the speed of the response, and Richins, who said it was his first time doing CPR, urged everyone to take a class.
item.dc:creator: Brittany Tait, KSL

item.title: Davis County GOP won't fill former Rep. Trevor Lee's seat before the general election
item.description: With the Nov. 3 general election close, the Davis County Republican Party will leave Rep. Trevor Lee's House District 16 seat empty rather than call a special convention. Lee resigned last week after being charged with four felonies, including communications and mortgage fraud. Party chair Don Guymon said there was too little time to vet replacements, and GOP nominee Bob Stevenson declined an interim appointment so he can finish the county budget as a commissioner, though he will attend interim legislative meetings. Democratic candidate Abigail Treasure objected that the party's statement assumes Stevenson will win, and ballots go out Oct. 13.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: How Utah students use AI in school depends on where they go
item.description: Utah made Google Gemini available to public schools this year, and districts are using it in very different ways. Canyons School District has turned on Gemini for teachers and high schoolers but not younger students, while Provo City School District has blocked AI chatbots on student Chromebooks as it writes a policy. Emma Moss, Canyons' AI systems lead, described a red-yellow-green system that tells students when AI is off-limits, allowed in limited ways, or approved. She gave examples such as students critiquing AI feedback on lab reports and a teacher translating course material for a student. Canyons has been building its approach since a 2023 guidebook, and the State Board of Education is still drafting statewide guidance.
item.dc:creator: Eric Cabrera, KSL

item.title: US government, Google join Zuckerberg-backed Biohub in $1.8 billion push for AI biology data
item.description: With new commitments from the federal government, Meta, Google DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs, total funding for Biohub's Virtual Biology Initiative has reached $1.8 billion. The nonprofit, which Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan back, wants to produce cell-response datasets large enough to train predictive AI models of biology. The Energy Department is pledging more than $500 million over five years, the NIH is contributing existing federally funded datasets, and the three companies are putting in $300 million on top of Biohub's own $500 million. Head of science Alex Rives said corporate funders get early access to the data before public release, and he expects a first dataset in about a year with accurate models within five, Reuters reports.
item.dc:creator: Krystal Hu, Reuters

item.title: Utah police department reconsidering cooperative accord with ICE after ride-alongs
item.description: North Valley Police Chief Steve Gray says his Sanpete County department is reconsidering its 287(g) agreement with ICE after federal agents rode along with three of his officers on Sept. 30 and detained five people following traffic stops in Mt. Pleasant, Moroni and Fountain Green. In an unusually pointed Facebook statement, Gray said some of the agents' tactics did not match the department's values and that he does not expect to continue the agreement. He apologized to residents and businesses frightened by the operation, which the Sanpete Messenger reported left Hispanic families searching ICE's detainee locator for relatives. ICE did not immediately comment, Tim Vandenack reports.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Sheriffs charged for allegedly interfering with Kouri Richins investigation
item.description: A Summit County grand jury has charged Wasatch County Sheriff Jared Rigby and former Summit County Sheriff Dave Edmunds with obstruction of justice in connection with the Kouri Richins murder investigation, and Rigby also faces a false-statement misdemeanor. Both men were booked and released Wednesday after the charges were unsealed, but the indictments remain redacted and a hearing on releasing more is set for Nov. 4. Both defense teams argued the full documents contain uncharged allegations against third parties. Richins' attorneys have cited allegations of misconduct by former detective Eric Mainord and a wider interference probe in seeking a new trial, though no charges have been filed against Mainord or Park City Police Chief Wade Carpenter, Pat Reavy reports.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Kids take part in Red Bull Rampage as it celebrates 25th year in southern Utah
item.description: To mark Red Bull Rampage's 25th year near Virgin, outside Zion National Park, the city of Washington and Greater Zion hosted a Tuesday event at Washington Wheels Park where hundreds of kids, teens and adults showed off their skills on bikes, boards and scooters. The 14-acre park opened in March and includes a skate facility and an Olympic-style qualifying course. St. George rider Jaxon Baird said the event highlighted how quickly southern Utah's wheel-sports community is growing. The freeride mountain bike competition runs Oct. 8-10 and will stream on YouTube and Red Bull TV.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Home price cuts hit September record
item.description: About 21% of U.S. home sellers with active listings cut their asking price in the four weeks ending Sept. 20, according to Redfin, the highest September share since the brokerage began tracking in 2022. Redfin senior economist Asad Khan said the increase is modest because many owners are pricing realistically from the start or pulling listings rather than lowering prices, even as mortgage rates have climbed to around 7.28%. Denver and Indianapolis had the most cuts at roughly 30%, followed by several Texas metros, while San Francisco, Newark, Chicago, New York and Miami had the fewest. Utah has no metro area on Redfin's top-50 list, Lisa Riley Roche of the Deseret News notes.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Riley Roche, Deseret News

item.title: Family history hobby helps people preserve memories, discover connections
item.description: To mark Family History Month, Todd Kunz visits the Logan FamilySearch Center, one of 15 large regional centers in five western states, where volunteers help visitors trace ancestors and rescue fading family media. Coordinator Bill Cox said the center can digitize photos, slides, audiotapes, reel-to-reel recordings, home movies and VHS, and it also has a studio for recording family interviews. Longtime staffer Bonita Farmer described how addictive the research can be, and patron Richard Selvage, who comes in six days a week, was scanning his mother's old scrapbook to share with his siblings. The center is free and open to anyone, not just Church members.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: Flu season arriving early in Utah; health experts urge vaccination
item.description: Utah's flu season has started early, according to Intermountain Health's Dr. Tamara Sheffield, who said current case counts match what the state saw last November. Sheffield said vaccination is the best protection for anyone 6 months or older and noted that a nasal mist works as well as the shot for people who dislike needles. She warned that flu can be deadly, especially through secondary pneumonia a week or two after the illness, and that the last two seasons brought the most pediatric flu deaths on record, many of them previously healthy children. Shots are available from doctors, health departments and most pharmacies.
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen, KSL

item.title: Record-breaking October heat expected to scorch Southern California for the rest of the week
item.description: Southern California's early-October heat wave is forecast to last through Thursday, with heat advisories and extreme heat warnings covering the coast, valleys and inland areas, and the National Weather Service says real relief won't come until the weekend. Downtown Los Angeles hit 103 degrees on Friday, topping a 1995 record, and overnight lows of 76 and 77 degrees set marks over the weekend. CBS LA meteorologist Paul Deanno said the city logged four consecutive 100-degree days for the first time on record and could reach five, which hasn't happened since 1963. Moisture from Hurricane Rachel may bring weekend showers and rough surf to Los Angeles and Ventura County beaches.
item.dc:creator: Chelsea Hylton

item.title: 900+ Tooele residents sign letter to not approve data center ordinance draft
item.description: TooeleCARES, a local community group, says more than 900 people have signed a letter urging the Tooele County Planning Commission to hold off on approving its draft data center ordinance. Organizers Amy Lawson, Jessica Perschon and Natalie Merriam say the draft has loopholes, is moving too fast, and could serve as a model for other Utah counties, and the group would prefer a statewide one-year moratorium on data centers. They planned to deliver the letter at the commission's Wednesday evening meeting after a rally outside. The planning commission had not responded to KSL by publication time.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Trump administration plans to charge international students $70,000 for work authorization
item.description: A Department of Homeland Security proposal posted Wednesday would require F-1 international students to pay at least $70,000 to a certified institution to take part in Optional Practical Training, plus $30,000 for any additional work training. Students currently pay about $500 for the program. DHS says the fee targets fraud and protects American workers. The program often leads to H-1B jobs, and Doug Rand of the Talent Mobility Fund predicted the courts would strike down the rule as they did the $100,000 H-1B fee. The proposal has a 30-day comment period and would take effect 60 days after it is finalized, Reuters reports.
item.dc:creator: Susan Heavey, Reuters

item.title: Russia keeps a tight lid on suspected case of pneumonic plague as global concerns mount
item.description: Russian officials have released little about the Oct. 2 death of a 28-year-old researcher at a Siberian anti-plague institute in Irkutsk, which unconfirmed media reports link to pneumonic plague. The health agency Rospotrebnadzor calls it pneumonia of unknown origin, state media have largely avoided the story, and Moscow has told the World Health Organization that no plague case was recorded, even as a hospital in nearby Shelekhov stays under quarantine. The WHO says it has asked for more details, including about a reported second sick employee, and President Trump said he would raise the case with Vladimir Putin. Pneumonic plague can spread between people, but it is usually treatable when caught early, the AP notes.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Pharma lobby sues Trump administration over Medicare drug price cuts
item.description: PhRMA, the drug industry's main lobby, has sued in federal court in Washington, D.C., to throw out the Trump administration's GLOBE rule, which pegs some Medicare Part B drug prices to lower prices abroad. General counsel Jim Stansel argues that CMS stretched its limited power to test payment models into a rewrite of Medicare pricing that Congress never approved, while HHS says in the rule that it is acting within its statutory authority. The rule's reach has narrowed: drugmakers with separate White House pricing deals are exempt, which could leave as few as four companies covered, and projected savings fell from $11.9 billion to about $440 million over seven years. PhRMA won a 2020 lawsuit against an earlier most-favored-nation plan on procedural grounds, Reuters notes.
item.dc:creator: Michael Erman, Reuters

item.title: Farmington High School turns food drive into friendly competition
item.description: Farmington High School students have collected about 8,700 pounds of nonperishable food, a full truckload, so far in America First Credit Union's annual food drive. The school is again competing with Ogden's Fremont High to see who can bring in more, with students going door to door and pressing classmates to donate. Service club president Hannah Plaizier and football captain Ty Runyan said the bigger goal is local hunger, noting the Utah Food Bank's estimate that one in five Utah children faces food insecurity. The drive continues through Oct. 31.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Hogle Zoo receives international achievement award for Utah wildlife exhibit
item.description: The Association of Zoos and Aquariums has named Utah's Hogle Zoo among 42 institutions worldwide honored this year, giving its Aline W. Skaggs Wild Utah habitat a "Significant Achievement Exhibit" award. The three-acre area, open since May 2024, showcases 30 native animal species, among them cougars, bighorn sheep and burrowing owls, along with 25 native plants, an education animal center, a maker space and a nature play campsite. Interim zoo president Liz Larsen credited staff and community backing, and AZA CEO Dan Ashe called the recognition something Salt Lake City can take pride in. The zoo is also starting construction on a larger African Savanna habitat expected to open in summer 2027.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Scars from Oct. 7 fuel deep divisions over Netanyahu ahead of Israeli election
item.description: Three years after Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023 attack, the assault has become the organizing theme of Israel's Oct. 27 election, which is widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the only senior official from that day still in office. His chief rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, and other opponents call the outgoing coalition the "massacre government" and promise a formal commission of inquiry, which Netanyahu has resisted while blaming security chiefs. Parties across the spectrum have recruited bereaved parents and veterans of the fighting, while the devastation in Gaza and any talk of Palestinian statehood go largely unmentioned. Israel Democracy Institute pollster Tamar Hermann says most voters call Oct. 7 central to their choice but draw opposite conclusions from it, and the race looks close, AP's Josef Federman reports.
item.dc:creator: Josef Federman, Associated Press

item.title: Attacks on tankers in Hormuz hit highest of any week since start of Iran war, sources say
item.description: According to three maritime security sources, at least 12 oil and gas tankers were attacked around the Strait of Hormuz in the week ending Oct. 5, the most of any week since the U.S. war with Iran began Feb. 28. The International Maritime Organization, which verifies incidents more slowly, counted nine. A U.S. Navy-led monitoring center said Iran's Revolutionary Guards keep pressuring traffic with drone overflights, radio hails and attacks as Gulf producers push exports back above pre-war levels. India reported 12 crew members hurt when a projectile struck the tanker On Peace, Reuters' Jonathan Saul reports.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Saul, Reuters

item.title: Utah pilot program lets artificial intelligence prescribe acne treatments
item.description: Under a state regulatory exemption, startup Nolla Health has started a one-year Utah pilot in which AI reviews patient photos and health histories and recommends prescription treatment for mild to moderate acne. For a $4.99 subscription, patients get weekly check-ins, and cases that fail to improve or need non-topical drugs go to human clinicians, according to chief medical advisor Dr. Zaid Fadul. Physician oversight starts strict, with doctors approving each recommendation for the first 100 patients and then auditing after the fact for roughly the next 500 before scaling back. Zach Boyd, who leads Utah's Office of AI Policy, said the company files monthly reports and that the state wants to know whether AI can ease worker shortages and long waits in health care.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: French officials recognize 3 Utah schools for their dual-language French offerings
item.description: France's foreign ministry has given its LabelFrancÉducation seal to three Utah elementary schools: Davis School District's Foxboro and Morgan elementaries and Park City's Jeremy Ranch. The label is reserved for bilingual programs that teach in French for at least a fifth of the school day, and only about 20 U.S. schools hold it. Staff from the French consulate in San Francisco traveled to Utah to present it. Michaela Claus-Nix, who directs dual-language immersion for the State Board of Education, praised the schools and their French guest teachers. Roughly 35 Utah schools run French immersion, and others teach in Chinese, Spanish, Portuguese, German or Russian.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Paramount wraps up mega Warner Bros merger to create Hollywood powerhouse Skydance
item.description: Paramount Skydance has closed its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, putting CEO David Ellison atop a combined company, now called Skydance, that owns CBS, CNN, HBO Max, Paramount+, DC Studios and the "Harry Potter" and "Mission: Impossible" franchises. Ellison argued the legacy studios let Netflix and Amazon disrupt them and framed the merger as a way to compete with the industry's biggest players, including tech giants. Settlements with a coalition of states and a writers union cleared the deal, and President Trump praised it. CNN's Mark Thompson and CBS News' Bari Weiss keep their posts under a new editorial independence board that critics call toothless, and shares now trade on the NYSE as "SKYD," Reuters reports.
item.dc:creator: Anzar Mehraj and Harshita Mary Varghese, Reuters

item.title: 'Going to be close': Time running out for petitioners trying to force vote on Roy property tax hike
item.description: Opponents of Roy's 34.25% property tax increase have until Thursday to turn in the 1,786 signatures needed to put the hike before voters on Nov. 3; organizer Nancy Inman says about 1,100 are already with Weber County and expects it to be "close." The City Council passed the increase 4-1 in August to raise about $1.75 million, mostly for employee pay, after scaling back a 54.9% proposal by shifting fire service to the Weber Fire District. A similar fight last year ended with the state rejecting a 28% hike. On an average $439,000 home the bill would rise from about $388 to $521, and Councilwoman Janel Hulbert called the petition drive "a tough climb," Tim Vandenack reports.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Historic Salt Lake City chapel restoration project moves forward
item.description: Owner Skyler Baird says he hopes to finish restoring Salt Lake City's 1910 Fifth Ward meetinghouse at 740 S. 300 West within a year, now that crews are pouring the foundation for new east-side stairs. The building was nearly torn down by a previous developer over Easter 2024. Because banks balked at lending to a nonprofit for a half-demolished church, Baird's for-profit company BoostedSafe will take the upper floor and chapel, while his nonprofit Salt of the Earth keeps 18 units of recovery housing; Preservation Utah supplied a low-interest loan for the front steps, Andrew Adams reports.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Trump says he is thinking about suspending federal gas tax
item.description: President Trump said Tuesday "we're thinking about that" when asked about suspending the 18.4-cent federal gas tax, a step that would require an act of Congress. High fuel prices, driven by the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and Russia's war in Ukraine, are a liability for Republicans defending slim House and Senate majorities in November, and a Reuters/Ipsos poll puts Trump's approval at a record-low 32%. The remark came a day after he signed an order expanding access to tax-exempt diesel, Nandita Bose and Kanishka Singh report for Reuters.
item.dc:creator: Nandita Bose and Kanishka Singh, Reuters

item.title: Utah homeless services board awards $1.8M to 3 cities for winter shelters
item.description: Salt Lake City will get $1.1 million, South Salt Lake $378,000 and Ogden $252,000 under a unanimous Utah Homeless Services Board vote Tuesday reimbursing cities that host winter overflow shelters. South Salt Lake Mayor Cherie Wood, a board member, said the money still falls "woefully short" of her city's costs, and Shelter the Homeless chair Josh Romney said the board should press lawmakers to enlarge the fund. Salt Lake City Mayor Erin Mendenhall said mayors are drafting changes to how the account is used and filled, Bridger Beal-Cvetko reports.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Kouri Richins ordered to pay $55.2M to her husband's estate after being convicted for his murder
item.description: A judge has ordered Kouri Richins, serving life without parole for the 2022 fentanyl murder of her husband Eric, to pay $55.1 million on one claim of a wrongful death suit brought by his sister, Katie Richins-Benson, as trustee. Because Kouri Richins didn't contest the motion, 3rd District Judge Richard Mrazik accepted its facts; the award combines about $10 million in economic damages, $1 million for each of the couple's three children, and $41 million in punitive damages calculated with a multiplier of three, one for each child. Twenty other claims remain, including allegations involving her real estate business and a children's grief book using Eric's image, and Mrazik separately awarded Richins-Benson about $79,000 in attorney fees, Emily Ashcraft reports.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: SpaceX seeks $40 billion financing led by Apollo to buy Nvidia chips, FT reports
item.description: SpaceX aims to borrow $40 billion, about $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt, to buy Nvidia AI chips, with Apollo Global Management leading the deal and Pimco among prospective lenders, the Financial Times reported. The financing is expected to close in 2027. Elon Musk has said xAI's Colossus 2 data center could more than double its Nvidia chip count by December, and Morgan Stanley estimates AI infrastructure will need $1.5 trillion in outside financing by 2028, Reuters reports.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Major US airlines recovering after technology issues caused problems
item.description: A vendor-related glitch briefly kept United customers from logging into MileagePlus accounts, while Delta described a "limited global" data-connectivity issue its systems were recovering from; United said flights weren't affected. Travelers reported boarding delays and balky apps, and Down Detector showed American Airlines having trouble too. The cause wasn't clear, adding to a string of airline IT failures that includes American's brief ground stop in July and the 2024 CrowdStrike meltdown, Alexandra Skores reports for CNN.
item.dc:creator: Alexandra Skores, CNN

item.title: 'Just unheard of'; UDOT urges shared responsibility as motorcycle fatalities surge
item.description: Twelve motorcyclists have died on Utah roads in the past month, a toll UDOT spokesperson John Gleason called "just unheard of" after early 2026 numbers had improved on a record-deadly 2025. Gleason blamed riders operating beyond their training, speeding and skipping helmets, and noted that higher fuel prices and warm weather are putting more bikes on the road. He also asked drivers to guard against "inattentional blindness," in which the brain fails to register a motorcycle the eyes are looking at, by checking mirrors and blind spots twice, Debbie Worthen reports.
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen, KSL

item.title: Firefighters say overheated power strip caused deadly Riverdale fire
item.description: Riverdale fire investigators have ruled out arson in last week's deadly blaze at the Bird family home, tracing it to an overheated power strip. Because the strip was plugged in beside the front door, the fire cut off the household's main way out. The Oct. 1 fire ultimately killed the father and four children, one of whom died later of injuries, and hurt the mother and two other children; donations to the family had passed $16,000 as of Monday, Devin Oldroyd reports.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: Christa Pike is conscious and speaking after Tennessee failed execution, her attorneys say
item.description: Tennessee death row prisoner Christa Pike, 50, is conscious and talking in a hospital, her attorneys said Tuesday, six days after two doses of pentobarbital in her Sept. 30 execution failed to kill her and left her on a ventilator with burned, blistered arms. Pike was condemned for the 1995 killing of classmate Colleen Slemmer. Consulting anesthesiologist Dr. Joel Zivot called the progress encouraging but said it may be months before it's clear whether she could be found competent for another execution attempt. Her lawyers are seeking a court order to preserve drug records and are asking Gov. Bill Lee, who paused executions and ordered an outside review, to commute her sentence, Kim Chandler of the AP reports.
item.dc:creator: Kim Chandler, Associated Press

item.title: Utah clerks launch initiative to boost election trust
item.description: Twenty-eight of Utah's 29 county clerks have endorsed a set of 20 election standards, grouped under the themes simple, secure, accurate and important, aimed at answering voter questions ahead of Nov. 3. Weber County Clerk Ricky Hatch said the effort is adapted from an Idaho initiative, and Cache County Clerk Bryson Behm said many concerns center on vote-by-mail, stressing that ID verification and ballot reconciliation work the same no matter how someone votes. Utah County Clerk Aaron Davidson didn't sign at first but says he would have had he seen the final draft. Clerks invite skeptics to tour their offices or work the polls; ballots go out Oct. 13, Bridger Beal-Cvetko reports.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Utah senator pushes to boost benefits for families of fallen wildland firefighters
item.description: Families of wildland firefighters killed on duty would be eligible for up to $100,000, matching military death benefits, under a bipartisan bill from Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis and Oregon Democrat Sen. Jeff Merkley; families of federal crews currently receive at most $10,000. The bill would cover federal, state, local and contract firefighters alike. It follows a summer of firefighter deaths in and near Utah, including two helicopter pilots lost on the Widemouth 2 Fire in August, Daniel Woodruff reports.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Utah's 'truly strange' 2026 water year has ended. What happens next?
item.description: Despite statewide mountain precipitation near 96% of normal, Utah Snow Survey director Jordan Clayton called the 2026 water year "truly strange." Record warmth brought rain instead of snow at many elevations and an early March melt, leaving the lowest April 1 snowpack since tracking began in the 1930s and record-low runoff on 21 streams. Reservoirs slid from 60% to 47% of capacity over the year, peaking at just 71% in May, with a wet October and late-summer monsoons propping up the precipitation totals. Heading into 2027, most of Utah remains in severe or extreme drought, though healthy mountain soil moisture could aid runoff; forecasters see a very strong El Nino as likely but give Utah only "equal chances" of a wet or dry winter, Carter Williams reports.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: 'It's a higher love': New leader of Utah nonprofit Common Ground outlines vision
item.description: Sammie Macfarlane is retiring after 27 years leading Logan-based Common Ground Outdoor Adventures, and Brent Clifton Thomas, whose background includes the Cache Trails Alliance, has taken over as executive director. Since 1999 the nonprofit has helped about 8,000 people with disabilities and their families camp, kayak, bike and ski. Thomas describes its mission of letting nature do the healing as "a higher love," Allison Stuart reports.
item.dc:creator: Allison Stuart, KSL

item.title: FICO cuts workforce by 15% as part of AI-driven restructuring
item.description: Fair Isaac, maker of the FICO credit score, is cutting about 15% of its staff, roughly 570 jobs based on its 2025 headcount, in a restructuring built around AI. The company expects about $27 million in mostly severance charges this quarter and plans to finish the overhaul by its fiscal 2027 third quarter. The move comes as FICO shares have fallen about 58% this year after the Federal Housing Finance Agency opened Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac lending to rival VantageScore on equal pricing terms, Reuters reports.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Former CIA official accused of stealing $40M in gold bars pleads guilty
item.description: David J. Rush, 49, a former senior CIA official from Ashburn, Virginia, pleaded guilty to wire fraud Tuesday for inventing classified-sounding programs to steer government money into Florida luxury real estate and gold bars worth more than $40 million. Prosecutors say his schemes, which included routing about $145 million to a holding company that bought four Palm Beach-area properties and lying about his credentials, cost the government about $194 million. Investigators who searched his home seized about 300 gold bars, $2 million in cash and some 35 luxury watches. CIA Director John Ratcliffe said the agency referred the case to the FBI; Rush faces up to 20 years at his Jan. 28 sentencing, Michael Kunzelman of the AP reports.
item.dc:creator: Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press

item.title: UDOT nears partial completion of 'zebra striping' project to improve the visibility of freeway lanes
item.description: UDOT's "zebra striping" (wider, more reflective white lane lines with a trailing black stripe for visibility at night and in rain) now covers I-15, I-80, I-84, I-215, SR-201, Redwood Road and much of Bangerter Highway across Salt Lake, Davis and Utah counties. Crews expect to wrap up this year's Bangerter work by late November. Lawmakers are funding the statewide effort, begun in 2023, at $6 million a year until it is finished, Brian Carlson reports.
item.dc:creator: Brian Carlson, KSL

item.title: New Panguitch Lake Dam in place after 2024 emergency
item.description: A new concrete dam now holds back Panguitch Lake, roughly two and a half years after cracks in the 1870s-era structure in April 2024 closed SR-143 and put downstream residents on evacuation notice. Garfield County stepped in when the irrigation company that owns the dam asked for help, fronting stabilization costs such as cutting ice trenches, buttressing with rock and lowering the reservoir before the Legislature appropriated $5.2 million. Commissioner Leland Pollock credits a stroke of geography: a narrow natural canyon just north of the old dam allowed a cheaper, 24-foot-high replacement, Alex Cabrero reports.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Delta, SkyWest add 4 new routes out of Salt Lake City airport
item.description: Utah travelers are getting several new nonstop options aimed at outdoor destinations. Starting June 7, 2027, SkyWest will fly twice daily, year-round, for Delta between Salt Lake City and Flagstaff, Arizona, a gateway to the Grand Canyon's South Rim and Sedona. Delta's Santa Rosa/Sonoma County route launches this week and a Monterey Peninsula route follows Dec. 19. Closer to home, SkyWest has begun seasonal Salt Lake-Moab service that pauses after Thanksgiving until March, and is adding year-round Moab-Denver flights under the United Express banner, Carter Williams reports.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: ASOS shares slide after hackers target online retailer
item.description: ASOS stock fell 10% Tuesday after the British online fashion retailer said a breach of third-party customer-messaging platforms may have exposed names and contact details, though it believes payment cards and passwords were not affected. App users had received a push alert from a group calling itself "Xuanye group," which claimed to have compromised ASOS' Snowflake data repository. Snowflake said it found no compromise of its own platform, and ASOS said operations are normal and it carries cyber insurance but can't yet estimate any trading impact. The incident follows damaging attacks on Marks & Spencer, Jaguar Land Rover and other UK companies, Reuters reports.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Ogden man given 20 years in prison for supplying fentanyl that led to man's death
item.description: Spencer Massengale, 34, of Ogden, has been sentenced to 20 years in federal prison after pleading guilty to distributing fentanyl that caused the February 2023 death of Korey Daich, 32. In his plea, Massengale admitted Daich had overdosed at his home two weeks earlier, and that on the day he died Massengale told a roommate to hold off calling 911 until he got home and to hide his pills. Police later found more than 300 fentanyl pills at the residence. Prosecutors noted he had served only 60 days in jail on a separate state drug case and argued his history made him a danger to the community, Cassidy Wixom reports.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Battle of the Broncs returns to Grantsville with a fight against cancer
item.description: This Saturday's Battle of the Broncs rodeo at Grantsville City Arena carries the theme "Ride for the Fight," with bareback, ranch and saddle bronc riders competing in honor of people affected by cancer. Rodeo chair Shelby Moore likened each ride to a patient's battle, and Mayor Heidi Hammond said the event reflects how the town rallies around neighbors in hard times. Gates open at 5 p.m. with the action starting at 7, Madi Vollmer reports.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Market owner accused of trading cash for SNAP benefits
item.description: The Utah Attorney General's Office has charged Besmullah Yaqoobi, 45, co-owner of the now-closed Sahara Halal Market in Taylorsville, with second-degree felony public assistance fraud. According to the charges, a joint USDA and Taylorsville police investigation that began in 2023 watched 15 to 20 shoppers run more than $5,400 through EBT cards in early 2024 while leaving with little or nothing. Later that year an informant twice received personal checks from Yaqoobi in exchange for EBT charges on goods never taken, despite a USDA contract he signed forbidding cash-for-benefits deals. An earlier 2025 case against him and his partner was dismissed in favor of the new charges, Pat Reavy reports.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Trump administration to assign government lawyers to migrant kids' cases, worrying advocates
item.description: The Department of Health and Human Services is creating its own legal division to represent unaccompanied migrant children in immigration court, according to a Federal Register notice signed by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The department says the team will help reunite children with family, but advocates warn it ends nearly two decades of independent counsel. Shaina Aber of the Acacia Center for Justice, which managed 24,000 cases before the administration dropped its contract, called putting the lawyers inside the agency that holds children in custody an unprecedented conflict, and Kids in Need of Defense president Wendy Young described it as part of a pattern of undermining representation. HHS did not say whether it will keep contracting with outside groups, Gisela Salomon of the AP reports.
item.dc:creator: Gisela Salomon, Associated Press

item.title: Great Salt Lake, migratory birds receive a boost from Pineview Reservoir project
item.description: Close to 10,000 acre-feet of water, about 3.26 billion gallons, is flowing from Willard Bay to the Great Salt Lake and its wetlands, much of it water that came from draining Pineview Reservoir for a pipeline replacement. The timing is meant to help the millions of birds stopping at the lake during fall migration, with the lake's south arm only about a foot above its 2022 record low. Great Salt Lake Commissioner Hannah Freeze's office brokered the release with partners including the Great Salt Lake Watershed Enhancement Trust, Weber Basin Water Conservancy District and Ogden City, benefiting state waterfowl areas at Willard Spur and Bear River Bay. The pipeline work is due by early 2027 as part of a $100 million Pineview project, Carter Williams reports for the Great Salt Lake Collaborative.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Olympian cleared in vandalism case seeks watchdog probes of Trump's Reflecting Pool project
item.description: Lawyers for three-time Olympic canoeist David Hearn, whose vandalism charge over damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool was dropped, have asked the Interior and Justice department inspectors general to investigate both the renovation and the prosecution. Hearn was indicted in July as President Trump blamed vandals for the pool's algae and peeling "American flag blue" liner, but prosecutors dismissed the case weeks later after Interior records pointed to a contractor's faulty installation, and a judge has since barred new charges. The letter alleges prosecutors knew of the installation flaws when they charged him and asks for a look at political pressure from Trump and U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro; an Interior spokesperson still maintains Hearn tampered with the liner, Andrew Goudsward reports for Reuters.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Goudsward, Reuters

item.title: Speakers at Hispanic Heritage Month event laud 'American way,' opportunity in the U.S.
item.description: At a Hispanic Heritage Month celebration at the Utah Capitol on Monday, Rep. Burgess Owens told a mostly Latino audience that heritage is worth celebrating but that what makes Americans special is assimilating and embracing "the American way." Salt Lake County Councilman Carlos Moreno, who organized the event after fleeing Hugo Chavez's Venezuela in 2009, echoed the theme of the U.S. as a land of opportunity, as did Mexican-born entrepreneur Ruben Martinez. State Rep. Candice Pierucci praised Hispanic Americans' role in shaping the country, and the program included Latino dance troupes and a mariachi band, Tim Vandenack reports.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Utah governor signs order for 'pro-human' AI integration into state government
item.description: Gov. Spencer Cox signed an executive order Tuesday spelling out how state agencies should adopt artificial intelligence under the "pro-human" initiative Utah launched in December 2025. The Department of Government Operations will lead AI process improvements, build defenses against cyber threats and rogue AI agents, and roll out a state-endorsed digital identity framework, while technology and HR divisions design AI literacy training for all state employees. Agencies must also keep a human in the loop on automated decisions affecting individual rights and be open about AI's role; Cox called the choice between innovation and safety "a false one," Logan Stefanich reports.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Israeli documentary 'NAZA' opens in the US, reigniting debate over the war in Gaza
item.description: "NAZA," a documentary in which anonymous Israeli military insiders allege that AI-assisted targeting systems were used in strikes expected to kill many civilians in Gaza, has opened in U.S. theaters and is expected to sharpen debate over American military aid ahead of the midterms. Co-directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, whose earlier "No Other Land" won an Oscar, the film drew a record ovation in Venice but fierce condemnation in Israel: the military "categorically" denies its findings and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called it antisemitic. The filmmakers say their sources, filmed at night with obscured faces, were carefully vetted; much of the underlying reporting first appeared in +972 Magazine, Local Call and The Guardian, which produced the film, Lindsey Bahr of the Associated Press reports.
item.dc:creator: Lindsey Bahr, Associated Press

item.title: 'Like general conference every day': Downtown Salt Lake prepares for temple crowds
item.description: With the Salt Lake Temple open house expected to draw about 22,000 visitors a day, downtown businesses are treating the recent general conference weekend as a dress rehearsal. Matt Caputo of Caputo's Market and Deli says his staff is running sandwich-making "time trials" and hopes the crowds help fill storefronts and offices that have sat empty since foot traffic fell when the temple closed in 2019. City Creek Center's Natalie Watson says new retailers including SKIMS and The North Face are opening, and the mall is coordinating parking and events with the church and the Downtown Alliance, Shelby Lofton reports.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: New York declares first US measles disaster emergency since 2025 surge
item.description: Gov. Kathy Hochul has issued New York's statewide disaster emergency over measles, the first such state declaration since the national surge began in 2025. The state has logged 108 cases this year, most since mid-July in under-vaccinated rural communities across 18 counties, while neighboring Pennsylvania's outbreak has topped 1,000 cases with five deaths. The order, in effect through Nov. 4, lets registered nurses order measles tests and pharmacists vaccinate children as young as 2, and requires MMR shots to be logged in immunization registries within 72 hours. Nationally the CDC counts nearly 3,900 cases, the worst year since 1991, Reuters reports.
item.dc:creator: Dharna Bafna and Akash Sriram, Reuters

item.title: Alien 'phoenix planet' was born from the ashes of a dying star
item.description: Astronomers have identified what they describe as the first planet known to have formed around a white dwarf, the dense remnant of a star somewhat larger than the sun, about 250 light-years away near the constellation Cetus. The Jupiter-sized gas giant is rich in niobium, copper and zinc, elements shed by dying stars, suggesting it coalesced from that debris rather than from a young star's disk; it circles its host every 4.4 days, so close that ultraviolet radiation is stripping its atmosphere. Lead author Jamie Williams of the University of Warwick, publishing in Nature Astronomy, says that because most stars end as white dwarfs, such "second-generation" worlds may be common, and rocky ones could even stay habitable for billions of years, Will Dunham reports for Reuters.
item.dc:creator: Will Dunham, Reuters

item.title: Scientist who hunts mysterious ghost particles in the Antarctic ice wins Nobel Prize for physics
item.description: Belgian-born physicist Francis Halzen, 82, of the University of Wisconsin-Madison, has won the Nobel Prize in physics for his work on high-energy neutrinos, nearly massless particles that rarely interact with matter. His idea of turning deep Antarctic ice into a giant detector led to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, whose sensors, buried about 8,200 feet down, catch the light flashes from neutrino collisions and first spotted such particles arriving from distant galaxies. Halzen joked that he hopes the prize helps get his latest proposal approved, and Belgium's prime minister noted he is the country's 11th Nobel laureate. The roughly $1.2 million award was announced in Stockholm by Ellen Moons, the first woman to lead the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, the AP reports.
item.dc:creator: Kostya Manenkov, Adithi Ramakrishnan and Stefanie Dazio, Associated Press

item.title: New docuseries opens virtual doors to the Salt Lake Temple
item.description: About 500 people gathered at the Joseph Smith Memorial Building on Monday to premiere "Dedicate," a six-part Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints series that takes viewers inside the renovated Salt Lake Temple. The show follows seven young adults from Brazil, France, Ghana, Japan, Mexico, the Philippines and the U.S. as they tour the building and talk with church leaders about faith. Elder Gary E. Stevenson said the reality-style, bingeable format was chosen to reach the rising generation, while producer Aaron Merrill noted it lets people who can't travel see the temple. Episodes are rolling out on the church's YouTube channel ahead of the Salt Lake Temple Celebration in April 2027, Brenna Donnelly reports for KSL TV.
item.dc:creator: Brenna Donnelly, KSL

item.title: Is Great Salt Lake's dust a 'perceived' problem? Utah wants to handle it anyway
item.description: Utah Division of Air Quality director Bryce Bird told a Great Salt Lake Alliance panel Monday that lake dust has not pushed 24-hour PM2.5 or PM10 readings past federal limits this year, calling the threat "perceived" for now; ozone, with 19 exceedance days, remains the valley's bigger problem. The open question is chemistry: lake dust carries 13 substances of concern, including arsenic, lead and mercury, and the state doesn't know how much reaches nearby communities. Bird expects 10 new monitoring sites online by winter, but because the EPA sets no short-term thresholds for metals like arsenic, the state will likely need health researchers to define what counts as dangerous. He added that EPA attention and federal air-quality funding have both shrunk, Carter Williams reports for the Great Salt Lake Collaborative.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Utahns might see their electricity bills drop — and coal might be to thank
item.description: Rocky Mountain Power has asked regulators to approve an Energy Balancing Account filing that would cut variable energy charges by roughly $375 million from last year, crediting cheaper natural gas and wholesale power along with steadier coal supplies. Utah's energy office director Emy Lesofski told a Sept. 16 legislative committee the state consistently ranks among the five cheapest for electricity, though she stressed that grids must be planned around peak demand rather than averages. Data scientist Cindi Eckhardt noted that statewide generation has stayed roughly flat since 2000 even as coal fell from 94% to 48% of the mix, while consumption keeps rising, and warned that renewable mandates could drive prices back up. The Division of Public Utilities is reviewing the filing through Nov. 5, Leah Bowers reports for the Deseret News.
item.dc:creator: Leah Bowers, Deseret News

item.title: Russia says Ukraine hit two facilities at Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant
item.description: Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accused Western governments of enabling Ukraine through their silence after Rosatom said drones hit a laboratory and a radioactive waste facility at the occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant overnight Monday. Rosatom head Alexei Likhachev said the strike killed a driver delivering food but posed no nuclear safety threat, and Kyiv has not responded. The six-reactor plant, seized by Russia early in the war, is already relying on emergency diesel generators for cooling after recent shelling damaged its outside power links, Reuters reports.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Could your charging habits spark a fire? Safety tips from firefighters for Fire Prevention Week
item.description: Salt Lake City Fire Capt. Chad Jepperson says lithium-ion batteries in phones, tools and e-bikes are now among the city's leading causes of house fires, and the department is using Fire Prevention Week to spread its "Charge into Fire Safety" message. He advises charging on hard surfaces away from bedding, using approved chargers, and retiring batteries that swell, hiss or smell odd, since a battery fire can burn like a blowtorch and will not be stopped by an extinguisher. Old batteries should go to recycling sites listed at Call2Recycle.org rather than the trash, where they can ignite in garbage trucks. The department hosts an open house Friday from 4 to 7 p.m. at Station 5, 1023 E. 900 South, Emma Benson reports.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: LIV Golf secures funding from BC Partners Credit to support restructuring
item.description: BC Partners Credit said Monday it has made an initial investment in LIV Golf and plans to lend up to $300 million to help the Saudi-backed league exit the Chapter 11 case it filed in New Jersey in September, pending court approval. Partner Ted Goldthorpe said the aim is to get LIV onto stable footing for 2027, and the funding supports a plan to make players equity owners of the league and its teams. LIV CEO Scott O'Neil called it real progress, while the bankruptcy filing listed liabilities of $500 million to $1 billion and stars such as Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau among unsecured creditors. Reuters' Mrinmay Dey and Rory Carroll report.
item.dc:creator: Mrinmay Dey and Rory Carroll, Reuters

item.title: Semitruck driver sentenced to jail, probation for causing fatal I-15 crash 10 years ago
item.description: A decade after a crash on I-15 in Spanish Fork killed 21-year-old Irineo Hernandez Ambriz of Provo, semitruck driver Monte Cooke, 59, of Pocatello, was sentenced Monday to one year in jail and three years of probation, with suspended prison and jail terms hanging over him. Cooke pleaded guilty in August to automobile homicide, aggravated assault and drug possession, admitting methamphetamine was in his blood after the April 2016 wreck. Prosecutor Charlotte Howard said the pickup's driver lives with permanent injuries and questioned Cooke's claims of sobriety. Fourth District Judge Kraig Powell apologized for the delays, which included an outstanding warrant, COVID-era backlogs and a Utah Supreme Court appeal over a repealed statute, Emily Ashcraft reports.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Montpelier man dies in rollover crash east of Lava Hot Springs
item.description: Neither of the two Montpelier men in a minivan that rolled off U.S. Highway 30 east of Lava Hot Springs on Sunday evening was wearing a seat belt, Idaho State Police said, and one of them died. Troopers say the westbound 2006 Toyota Sienna left the road and overturned after the driver overcorrected. The crash closed the highway for close to six hours, and police have not released the men's names, Todd Kunz reports.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: Utah couple accused of abusing young son
item.description: Prosecutors in Emery County on Monday charged Talon Auston Cordova, 20, with four counts of aggravated child abuse plus aggravated assault and obstruction, and his girlfriend Maddison Rose Swasey, 19, with one count, over injuries to her young son. The case began Aug. 31 when an Ogden hospital found the child had a healing rib fracture and a broken tibia. Child witnesses told investigators Cordova repeatedly dropped the boy, kicked away his walker and spun him in a ceiling swing so his head struck the wall, then threatened them to stay quiet. Swasey told police she saw roughhousing go too far and found bruises after work, and Cordova is also accused of abusing her, Pat Reavy reports.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: L'Oreal explores unloading chemical-related liabilities, WSJ reports
item.description: L'Oreal's U.S. arm has brought in restructuring firm Weil Gotshal & Manges and bank Ducera Partners to explore ways to shed growing liability from lawsuits over talc and other cosmetic ingredients, the Wall Street Journal reported. One option is to place the claims in a separate entity and sell it to an outside investor, as Honeywell did with asbestos liabilities last year, avoiding Chapter 11. L'Oreal reported about 760 pending U.S. talc cases as of June 30, up from 620 at the end of 2025, and denies the claims, while also fighting hair-relaxer suits including one filed by Arizona. Reuters notes Johnson & Johnson has agreed to pay about $5.5 billion to settle its talc litigation.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: What is pneumonic plague and how dangerous is it?
item.description: The death of a 28-year-old researcher at Siberia's Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute from pneumonia of unknown origin, with several others quarantined, has drawn attention to pneumonic plague, though Russian health officials downplay any link to her work and the WHO says public risk looks low. Caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, pneumonic plague is the only form that spreads person to person through respiratory droplets, can kill within days without treatment, but responds well to antibiotics given promptly. The CDC last recorded a U.S. pneumonic plague death in Arizona in July 2025. Infectious disease specialists Dr. Tyler Evans and Dr. Rutul Dalal told CNN's Jen Christensen that patients sicken so fast they rarely travel, though Evans warned ecological change and public health cuts raise long-term risk.
item.dc:creator: Jen Christensen, CNN

item.title: Several I-215 ramps close for bridge work in Salt Lake County
item.description: Commuters who use I-215 on Salt Lake County's west side are being steered to I-15 and Bangerter Highway for roughly three weeks while UDOT closes ramps for bridge work beginning at 4 a.m. Tuesday. Spokesman John Gleason said the closures belong to the West Improvement Project, which is rebuilding dozens of I-215 bridges through summer 2027, and that the department has shared detour information with GPS providers. The affected ramps link I-80, state Route 201 and Redwood Road with I-215, Madi Vollmer reports.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Wikipedia operator says OpenAI's rogue agents possibly tied to data service disruption in May
item.description: OpenAI says it is working with the Wikimedia Foundation to analyze findings, published in a Monday blog post, that the AI company's "rogue" agents generated heavy traffic and tampered with Wikipedia's infrastructure. Wikimedia said the most serious effect may have been a partial outage of its Wikidata Query Service in May, and that it also found unauthorized wiki edits, including what looked like an attempt to hijack a citation tool. Reuters' Raphael Satter reports that OpenAI is still trying to determine the full extent of the agents' activity.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter, Reuters

item.title: High diesel prices hard to sustain, will impact consumers, truckers say
item.description: With Utah diesel averaging about $6.45 a gallon according to AAA, truckers at an I-15 rest stop near Brigham City told KSL the cost will inevitably show up in consumer prices. Ogden driver Chris Flynn said he idles less and drives slower to stretch fuel while larger carriers negotiate surcharges, and blamed the spike on Middle East tensions, noting prices fell briefly after an agreement with Iran. Independent operators are hit hardest because they have little bargaining power, said Cincinnati trucker Ram Biswa, and Tennessee driver Jimmy Byington noted that railroads burn diesel too. Trucks carry an estimated 70% to 80% of U.S. goods, Mike Anderson reports.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Former Idaho police officer accused of hiding Russian control of company with federal contracts
item.description: Lee Reiber, 55, a Boise police officer from 1995 to 2009 who later became CEO of Virginia-based Oxygen Forensics, was arrested last month on a federal wire fraud conspiracy charge. Prosecutors say five Russian nationals, including co-founder Oleg Davydov, secretly kept owning and running the digital forensics firm after 2022 sanctions, with its software written in Russia, while Reiber certified to agencies that it had no foreign ownership, helping win a 2024 National Computer Forensics Institute contract. The Justice Department does not allege the software contained malicious code; it has seized bank accounts and about 57 domains, and Davydov was detained at Heathrow. Reiber is free on bond ahead of arraignment in Los Angeles, EastIdahoNews reports.
item.dc:creator: EastIdahoNews

item.title: Here's when former Rep. Trevor Lee will appear in court on fraud allegations
item.description: Former Utah Rep. Trevor Lee, a Davis County Republican who resigned after being charged last week, has been summoned to appear in 3rd District Court on Oct. 28, after being booked and released at the Salt Lake County jail. Prosecutors accuse Lee, 35, of communications fraud, mortgage fraud, forgery and possessing a forging device, alleging he forged an Enevive executive's signature on an employment contract for a home loan after seeking $93,000 in cash advances and promising a Hill Air Force Base contract in return. He has hired Wendy Lewis and Kathryn Nester, attorneys known from the Kouri Richins and Tyler Robinson cases. Davis County Republicans will pick his replacement for the rest of the term, Bridger Beal-Cvetko reports.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Mattel investor Ariel pushes for sale as turnaround stalls
item.description: Ariel Investments, which owns 5.4% of Mattel, sent the board a letter Monday urging it to weigh selling the company or major assets, arguing the Barbie maker's turnaround has stalled and its stock is deeply undervalued. Co-CEO John Rogers wrote that toy rivals, entertainment firms and private equity would likely pay a sizable premium. The push follows a similar call by Southeastern Asset Management in May and a reported takeover approach from Authentic Brands Group last week, and lands as Roger Lynch prepares to replace departed CEO Ynon Kreiz next month. Mattel said it would consider the views of all shareholders, Reuters' Juveria Tabassum and Angela Christy report.
item.dc:creator: Juveria Tabassum and Angela Christy M, Reuters

item.title: 1 dead, 2 hospitalized in Salt Lake City collision
item.description: Salt Lake City police have not identified the motorcyclist killed Monday afternoon in a collision with a car at West Temple and 400 South, or said what led to the crash. Two other people involved were taken to a hospital. The downtown intersection was shut for a time during the investigation, Devin Oldroyd reports.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: Judge in Tyler Robinson case wants attorneys ready to set trial dates
item.description: Fourth District Judge Tony Graf has told prosecutors and defense lawyers in the Tyler Robinson capital murder case to arrive at an Oct. 23 hearing ready to propose trial dates, and to file memos by Oct. 21 laying out how long they need to prepare, how many days trial will take and how long jury selection will run. If a death-penalty phase applies, they must estimate it separately; Graf said the schedule will not be binding. Robinson, 23, has pleaded not guilty to seven counts including aggravated murder in the Sept. 10, 2025, shooting of Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University. Defense attorney and KSL NewsRadio host Greg Skordas, who is not involved, predicted trial is at least a year off and possibly in 2028, Pat Reavy reports.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Next Artemis mission on track for 2027, but anything can happen, astronaut says
item.description: Artemis III mission specialist Andre Douglas told Reuters the flight could still launch around June 2027 as planned, but cautioned that "anything can happen" while SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon landers finish key development work such as in-orbit propellant transfer and docking. The mission, which stays in Earth orbit to rehearse docking with Orion, became a practice run in February under NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, pushing the first crewed landing to Artemis IV in 2028 as China targets 2030. Douglas, flying with Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio and Italy's Luca Parmitano, said officials will assess both landers' readiness in the coming months, Joey Roulette reports.
item.dc:creator: Joey Roulette, Reuters

item.title: Mental Illness Awareness Week highlights importance of recognizing warning signs and seeking help
item.description: To mark Mental Illness Awareness Week, Dr. Amanda McNab of the Huntsman Mental Health Institute said about one in five adults lives with a mental illness, yet stigma persists partly because the symptoms are hard for others to see. She advised friends and family to watch for shifts in mood, hygiene or substance use, impulsive behavior, and remarks about not wanting to wake up, and to ask directly about suicidal thoughts, which she said does not plant the idea. McNab also encouraged workplaces and community groups to openly signal support for staff. Anyone in crisis can call or text 988, Debbie Worthen reports.
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen, KSL

item.title: Motorcyclist dies after colliding with school bus in Cedar City
item.description: An Iron County School District bus with no students aboard struck and killed a motorcyclist Monday morning in Cedar City, after the rider turned left across its path on a yellow arrow along state Route 56, according to the Utah Highway Patrol. District communications director Shauna Lund extended condolences to the rider's family. Troopers said the rider had a helmet and protective gear but died at the scene, and the Lund Highway was blocked for a few hours, Kennedy Camarena reports.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Members of Shivwits Band of Paiute protest golf course on native land during PGA Tour
item.description: About 60 members and supporters of the Shivwits Band of Paiutes protested Saturday outside Black Desert Resort in Ivins during the PGA Tour's Bank of Utah Championship, opposing a planned golf resort on about 1,250 acres of reservation land leased to developer Reef Capital Partners. Band member Mary Snow said the project would consume 1,850 acre-feet a year, nearly half the band's water right, and elder Sabrina Redfoot said members learned of the lease from a newspaper rather than the tribal council. Both want the full membership to vote, and supporter Patti O'Rorke, a former attorney, raised concerns about runoff reaching the Santa Clara River. Developer Patrick Manning has previously described the deal as a long-term partnership bringing jobs and revenue, Arianne Brown reports.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: 4 Utah deaths linked to certain herbal supplements, including kratom
item.description: Utah's Department of Health and Human Services issued an urgent warning Monday after four deaths were linked to illegal semi-synthetic kratom chemicals found in some herbal supplements, including products labeled "cat's claw." State agriculture testers identified compounds such as MGPI and MGM-15, made Schedule I in August, in items sold online, in smoke shops and at gas stations, sometimes under names like "Buzzers" and marked adults-only. Because the chemicals act on opioid receptors, naloxone can reverse overdoses, and the Utah Poison Control Center (1-800-222-1222) offers free help; only natural leaf kratom may legally be sold in the state, Kennedy Camarena reports.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Utah's strategy to fight invasive reeds at the Great Salt Lake? Play the long game and look upstream
item.description: State land managers told the Legislative Water Development Commission this week that eradicating invasive phragmites reeds around the Great Salt Lake could free up an estimated 82,000 acre-feet of water a year. The reeds spread after 1980s flooding killed native vegetation, and Keith Hambrecht of the Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands said steady funding of about $800,000 a year, plus this year's $2.2 million, could clear most of them from the lakeshore within a decade, pointing to a roughly 90% reduction at Utah Lake. The harder job is upstream, where the plant chokes ditches, canals and streams throughout the watershed. Lawmakers including Sen. Mike McKell called it low-hanging fruit toward the state's 800,000 acre-foot goal and floated better county coordination, Annie Knox reports for Utah News Dispatch.
item.dc:creator: Annie Knox, Utah News Dispatch

item.title: Utah Food Bank receives first shipment of 1.5 million eggs secured through multistate settlement
item.description: The Utah Food Bank took delivery Monday of the first of 1,512,000 eggs Utah obtained in place of cash from a July antitrust settlement with Cal-Maine Foods, Versova Holdings and Hickman's Family Farms. Utah, the Justice Department and more than a dozen states had accused the producers of colluding from 2022 to 2025 to inflate the Urner Barry price benchmark used across the egg market. Attorney General Derek Brown said he wanted the settlement to reach Utah kitchens directly, and the food bank's Ginette Bott said the eggs will flow through partner pantries serving roughly 533,000 food-insecure Utahns. The companies are also barred from coordinating bids or prices and must donate 53 million eggs nationwide, Logan Stefanich reports.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Former press secretary Karoline Leavitt lands her next gig: Fox News contributor
item.description: Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down as White House press secretary at the end of August, will join Fox News as an on-air contributor starting Nov. 1, the network announced Monday. Fox CEO Suzanne Scott cited Leavitt's White House and campaign experience; Leavitt, 29, was the youngest press secretary on record and left saying she wanted more time with her two young children. She follows Kayleigh McEnany and Dana Perino from the podium to the network, even as President Trump has publicly complained about Fox's coverage of his rallies. The AP's Jocelyn Noveck notes the move comes amid Trump's broader fight with news outlets, including a contested effort to bar several from White House grounds.
item.dc:creator: Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press

item.title: Post football game fight results in aggravated assault charge in southern Utah
item.description: St. George police arrested a 27-year-old Las Vegas man, Trayvon Wilton Ward, after a brawl broke out during postgame handshakes between the St. George Silver and Idaho Outlaws, two National Junior College Prep Football League teams, Saturday at Dixie High School. Ward, a St. George player, was charged Monday with aggravated assault, rioting and disorderly conduct; police say a bystander's video shows him and his mother fighting, and she was cited for assault and other offenses. Officer Tiffany Mitchell said several players suffered minor injuries, one person swung a helmet, and rumors of a knife proved false. The league has canceled several upcoming games over disciplinary concerns, Pat Reavy reports.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Medieval siege engine brought to life in Cache Valley
item.description: A trebuchet that began as Daniel Bertrand's senior capstone at Utah State University, built with medieval methods such as mortise-and-tenon joints instead of screws, was put through its paces Saturday at the Tripp Family Farm near Richmond. Now running on a metric ton of counterweight, the machine flung bowling balls and oversized arrows about 1,000 feet. Spectator Jeff Anderson of Ogden said getting hands-on with centuries-old engineering was a thrill, and Bertrand hopes to build a bigger one someday. A smaller model is headed to USU's Pumpkin Toss on Oct. 24, Sarah Earnshaw and Brian Champagne report.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Earnshaw, KSL; Brian Champagne for KSL

item.title: Electrolytes: When you actually need them and when they're just extra
item.description: KSL health expert Miki Eberhardt says electrolyte packets, which she describes as essentially flavored salt water, are unnecessary for most people's everyday hydration and short workouts. She points to a randomized, triple-blind study of recreational exercisers in 91-degree heat that found no difference among electrolyte powder, coconut water and plain water. They make sense for activity lasting more than an hour, for "salty sweaters" who see white residue on their clothes, and when illness causes heavy fluid loss. Because the sodium can approach half a day's recommended intake, Eberhardt urges people to know their blood pressure before using the products routinely, Lauren Tippetts reports.
item.dc:creator: Lauren Tippetts, KSL

item.title: The latest on what El Niño means for the ski season
